Iran: The Latest
Iran's Trump assassination plot & Houthis restart Yemen war
Iran’s proxy group the Houthis have launched fresh missile attacks on Yemeni ports in the Red Sea as their conflict with Saudi Arabia heats up. A new war in the Arabian Peninsula is now inevitable, according to former Yemeni diplomat Mahmoud Shehrah.
On today’s episode of Iran: The Latest, Roland Oliphant talks to Chatham House’s Shehrah to unpack the Houthis' intentions and to what extent they are acting on Tehran’s orders. Could they close the Bab al-Mendab strait and what can the West do about it?
Plus, news of an Iranian assassination plot against Donald Trump that forced him to hide in an airplane catering trolley, and why the US president is now demanding war reparations from Iran to resolve their dispute over the Strait of Hormuz.
Highlights
- Iran’s proxy group the Houthis restarting the Yemen war
- Iran's Trump assassination plot exposed

sources.news_title: The Iran War Is Going So Well That Trump Had to Hide in an Airport Catering Truck
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
After the NATO summit in Turkey last month, Donald Trump pulled up in a limo, climbed the stairs to the blue-liveried door of Air Force One, then turned and waved. The plane took off from Ankara 20 minutes later, ferrying the president, his entourage, and the journalists who had covered his trip.
Or so it seemed. In truth, as the Washington Post revealed last night, the White House had pulled a switcheroo. A surreptitious airport catering truck secretly shuttled Trump to a waiting military plane, which flew him out instead. By itself, the story is a bizarre chapter in presidential history. But the context of the bait and switch—including the assassination threat that preceded it, an evident comfort with deceiving and potentially endangering members of his own administration and the press, and even controversy surrounding Air Force One itself—also marries a few themes of Trump’s second term so far.
This sounds like something out of a spy movie. Tell me more!
Here’s what we know. The catering truck, which typically loads in-flight meals, parked on the right side of Air Force One, partially shielded from media cameras. According to the Post, Trump crossed to the other side of the presidential plane after boarding and stepped into the truck’s elevated container. Video shows a suited man climbing into the vehicle’s cab, the container lowering, and the truck pulling away. It then sidles up to a smaller U.S. government jet and elevates its container once again, presumably letting Trump board unnoticed. The smaller plane then flew to the U.K., where Trump stopped en route to Washington, under a nondescript call sign. To help conceal the plot, which one anonymous U.S. official called a “deception operation,” White House officials made journalists aboard Air Force One close their window shades. Once in Britain, according to the New York Times, Trump was covertly ferried back to Air Force One as though he had been aboard the whole time.
That’s pretty elaborate! But why do this? You mentioned something about an assassination threat …?
One doesn’t play Schrödinger’s president just for fun. U.S. officials allegedly devised the ruse after they became concerned about an Iranian threat to target Trump as he left Turkey, which borders Iran. The Wall Street Journal reported today that the intelligence came from Israel and included a threat to shoot shoulder-to-air missiles at Air Force One.
So, besides lying to journalists aboard, the administration basically used them as bait?
You could say that. Journalists—and even some lower-level Trump officials—didn’t realize that the president wasn’t really on the plane with them. Nor were they told of the threat that prompted the switcheroo. Later, asked why reporters had had to close their window shades when leaving Turkey, Trump failed to mention that he had switched flights. “I’m No. 1 on their list,” he said, referring to Iran. “But if I go, you go. Right?” As it turns out, maybe not.
That’s dark. Has anything like this happened before?
Sort of. U.S. presidents rarely travel without journalists, and it’s even rarer for administrations to conceal the president’s true location. Officials were vague about George W. Bush’s whereabouts immediately after the Sept. 11 attacks, and Bill Clinton took an unmarked plane from India to Pakistan in 2000. But even Bush had reporters with him, and Clinton’s staff told at least one journalist about the switch beforehand. Joe Biden’s clandestine 2023 train trip to Ukraine involved a false public schedule, but it also included two journalists—and everyone else found out about it as soon as Biden arrived. Per the Times, though, the Secret Service has occasionally used decoy flights or motorcades to protect presidents.
So is this just a case of liberals criticizing Trump for something other presidents have done?
Presidents rightly expect more security than the rest of us, but that typically comes with greater scrutiny of their locations and activities too. Journalists wrist-slapped Barack Obama in 2010 after he briefly slipped the press pool in Washington to attend his daughter’s soccer game. In Trump’s case, his status near an active war zone was unknown to even senior U.S. officials for hours—and was kept hidden from the public until reporters exposed it more than a month later.
Wait a sec: I remember Trump bragging about a new plane he got from Qatar. So why was the old Air Force One the decoy in this case?
Good memory. Trump flew into Turkey on a luxury Boeing jet that Qatar’s government gave him last year, an offering that was widely seen as a bribe. But on July 8, as the NATO summit ended, the president posted that he would be leaving aboard the older Air Force One, which is still decked out in its Kennedy-era color scheme, “for old time’s sake.” The stated reason was to let U.S. troops at a British base tour the Qatari-gifted aircraft, which had been freshly repainted in red, white, blue, and gold. (This is Trump’s plane, after all.) But as the Times later revealed, the truth was more sinister. Trump’s demands to quickly retrofit the Qatari plane had apparently left it without sophisticated defensive systems, making it more vulnerable to Iranian attacks. The Times reporting enraged Trump, and the administration tried to unmask the paper’s sources before ultimately backing down. In retrospect, though, the president’s post was likely part of the gambit, helping him slip away aboard an entirely different plane.
Speaking of Iran: How is Trump’s war going?
If having to conceal himself inside a catering truck is any indication, not well. The Iranian assassination threat came after the president’s ceasefire fell apart. Since then, the two sides have continued to trade attacks. As my colleague Fred Kaplan explained yesterday, Iranian hard-liners want to keep control of the Strait of Hormuz, a key trade route. Trump, apparently wary of escalating the fight, is hoping that Iran’s economy will collapse. On Tuesday, an American helicopter appeared to have fired a missile at a Panama-flagged container ship that tried to break the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. In short, lasting peace seems further away than ever.
In case you’d prefer not to keep picturing our president perched on a pile of in-flight meals, my colleagues have some other ideas about how to spend the rest of your evening:
Rediscover the power of serendipity: Longtime Slatester Dan Kois is your tour guide on a journey back in time to rediscover the lost art of hanging out as it was practiced in 1996, the year of Slate’s birth. The first challenge centers on the one part of Friends that was 100 percent accurate. (Sign up here to get all the challenges in your inbox as they roll out over the coming weeks!)
Check out a genre-spanning series: Slate book critic Laura Miller has a tried-and-true suggestion if you’re in need of summer reading material. Robert Jackson Bennett’s fascinating Ana and Din series deftly blends fantasy and mystery, and luckily for us, a new installment just published. Laura has recommended these books over and over, and they’ve proved to be a hit with everyone.
Enjoy some low-stakes WFH drama: What should you do when cats (and their butts) take center stage during Zoom meetings? A manager wrote in to Slate’s Good Job column for help with a delightfully silly workplace issue: “I don’t want to take away something that brings my employee joy, but I’m also tired of looking at cat butts when we’re trying to accomplish something.” Doree Shafrir offers some purrfect advice.
Unwind with a classic game: Five letters for “Event on the campaign trail”? Eleven letters for “Movie villain described by Tobe Hooper as a ‘big baby’ ”? Three letters for “Uhh …”? If these clues get your neurons firing, you’ll love our daily crossword!
That’s it for me! Enjoy the rest of your night, and see you tomorrow.

sources.news_title: Maddow, O'Donnell Giddy About Iranian Assassination Plot Against Trump
sources.text:
An Iranian assassination plot against President Trump was apparently so credible that while leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month, the Secret Service deemed it necessary to play a shell game with Air Force One and spirited away the President to a different Air Force plane. However, to the leftist extremists of MS NOW, it was rollicking affair. During the handoff between Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O’Donnell’s The Last Word Monday night, the two laughed about situation and reveled in how Trump “lost complete control in this story.”
“I am very pleased,” Maddow proclaimed as she proceeded to explain how excited she was about the story and about getting to listen to O’Donnell rant about it:
I am very pleased to say it's time for The Last Word with Lawrence O'Donnell. Which is more of a pleasure for me to say than usual, because The New York Times has just posted a headline on the front page of the New York Times website, which reads, "Trump hid in a catering container to sneak out of Turkey.”

sources.text:
“If I go, you go” – the words you might not want to hear from a president you’ve just travelled with on a decoy plane after security threats from the Iranian regime for your original flight. Or so you thought.
It turns out that when Donald Trump travelled back to the US from a Nato summit in Ankara last month, he actually wasn’t on the plane with his White House staff and the journalists who had been told he was.
They became the decoy, while the President was smuggled on a third plane, inside a Turkish food truck. This is how it all unfolded.

sources.news_title: Trump smuggled off Air Force One in catering truck over Iran threat
‘Deplorable’: Trump’s Secret Escape Caught on Video After Reporters Allegedly Left as Bait for Attack, Now White House Wants the Whole Thing Buried
sources.text:
In a stunning revelation, President Donald Trump endangered the lives of the White House press corps after the NATO summit in Turkey last month when administration officials allegedly lied about how Trump was planning to leave the country.
The president’s whole story about flying from Turkey to England aboard an older yet more secure Air Force One jet was just a smokescreen, which unraveled in spectacular fashion when video footage of how Trump really traveled to England surfaced, according to reporting from The Washington Post and New York Times.
Video of the baby blue older version of Air Force One in Ankara shows catering containers used for transporting meals on the opposite side of the plane from where the president and reporters boarded.
The president flew into Turkey on July 7 for the summit in Ankara on July 8 aboard his new Air Force One luxury Boeing 747, a gift from Qatar’s royal family in 2025.
Trump used the luxury jet from Qatar for the first time to travel to the summit after spending hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars upgrading security on the jet.
But after the summit, The New York Times reported, supposed threats from Iran and security concerns about the new plane caused Trump to switch back to an older model of Air Force One with better security upgrades for a trip to Mildenhall Air Base in England before Trump’s return to the U.S.
At the time, Trump officials said the president wanted U.S. troops in England to see the new Air Force One before he took it home.
But it turns out, while Trump boarded the older Air Force One in Ankara as usual with reporters in tow, he secretly left the plane via a catering container and boarded a waiting military jet, leaving the press and some administration staffers to travel aboard the potential Iranian target, the news outlets reported.
Once in England, the administration engaged in another astonishing ruse to return Mr. Trump to Air Force One so that it appeared that’s how he had flown to the United Kingdom and from which he deplaned as usual.
“Mr Trump was brought by vehicle from the third plane that he had arrived on to the older Air Force One, boarded it through a different entrance and strode down the step from the upper left-side door as he would typically do, according to [a] US official,” The New York Times reported.
Trump then returned to the U.S. aboard the Qatari luxury jet.
Social media exploded in outrage and fury over Trump and his administration’s duplicitousness.
“So Trump and the White House lied about which plane Trump was on flying out of Turkey, setting up journalists who thought they were on the same plane as the president to possibly be the target of an Iranian attack while he secretly departed on a different one. Words fail,” journalist Aaron Rupar noted in a post on Threads.
This commenter voiced serious anger over Trump’s astonishing secret plane switch.
“The word ‘deplorable’ doesn’t begin to describe this miserable excuse of a human.”
Threads user Gary Stweart wondered, “So they were expecting the whole plane to blow up and take all the media with it. What a prick.”
Reporters asked the White House on Monday about the secret flight from Turkey to England.
Communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, according to The Guardian, that the Qatari jet “has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.”
“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” he said.
In addition to all the taxpayer money Trump spent to upgrade the Qatari luxury jet, he has said he plans to take it with him when he leaves the White House in 2029 for a display at his future Miami-based presidential library. Critics, though, believe he plans to keep it for his own personal use when his presidency ends.

sources.news_title: Trump Used Air Force One Passengers As Decoys, Saved Himself
sources.text:
At first glance, reports that President Trump secretly slipped off Air Force One in a catering truck to thwart an Iranian assassination threat sound like a blockbuster political thriller come to life. Upon closer examination, this is almost the exact opposite of President Harrison Ford heroically ditching his escape pod so he could stay aboard Air Force One, personally fighting off a band of terrorists, and saving as many passengers as possible with little concern for his own life.
Trump’s July 8 plane escapade always sounded fishy. After flying to a NATO summit in Turkey on his new $400 million luxury jet from Qatar, Trump opted to fly home on the older Air Force One. Trump claimed, absurdly, that U.S. troops stationed in U.K. really wanted to check out the new Qatari aircraft, so “for old time’s sake, we’ll be taking the former Air Force One.”
Later that day, the New York Times reported that the switch was really motivated by concerns that the Qatari jet’s security features weren’t up to snuff. Officials told the outlet that changing planes was a “precautionary measure made at the advice of the Secret Service and not because of a specific threat.”
It turns out none of that was accurate. In recent weeks, the Times and CBS News reported that the president actually changed planes in response to a credible threat that Iran and its proxies were targeting his Air Force One flight. And on Monday, the Washington Post revealed that Trump participated in an elaborate ruse to dodge the potential Iranian plot.
After boarding the older Air Force One in Ankara, Trump and a few aides secretly exited the aircraft on a catering truck, which then ferried them to a nearby Air Force C-32A:
To exit that plane without being seen by those uninvolved in the operation, Trump and several aides stepped aboard an airport catering truck, which was elevated plane-side using hydraulics and positioned at a door on the opposite side of Air Force One’s entrance, according to the U.S. official and other corroborating material.
Imagery captured by the news media at the Turkish airport shows a staircase on one side of the legacy Air Force One and the catering truck on the other, with its container elevated to the level of the plane. Trump arrived in a limousine, climbed the staircase and waved toward the tarmac as he boarded, video shows.
A few minutes later … a man in a suit entered the catering truck’s cab, according to media pool video of the departure process. The container was lowered into the bed of the vehicle, which then pulled away from Air Force One and drove to the smaller C-32A nearby, the video appears to show. The truck is out of view for about 40 seconds when the camera pans away and is briefly hidden while behind the C-32A’s engines.
Video shows members of the White House press corps boarding the back of Air Force One as Trump was secretly whisked away. Then both the Trump-less Air Force One and the C-32A flew to Britain. It’s unclear how the president reentered Air Force One undetected after landing, but he was seen exiting that plane around 10:56 p.m.
Obviously, the Secret Service’s top priority is keeping the president safe, and they couldn’t announce, “Heads-up, we’re switching planes to trick the Iranians!” But this escapade raises a lot of questions. Why did they let the press and some White House staffers board an Air Force One flight that was potentially being targeted by Iran? Did they even try to come up with a way to save everyone? Presumably Trump wouldn’t care that much about putting the “enemy of the people” in harm’s way. But did he raise any concerns about leaving some of his staffers on a dangerous flight? How did they choose whom to put on the C-32A? How do their colleagues feel about unknowingly serving as Trump’s decoys?
One thing that is clear: Trump is not the guy you want for your secret mission. Incredibly, he did manage not to publicly brag about deceiving the Iranians for a whole month. But he made some eyebrow-raising comments to reporters while joining them for the flight back from Britain on the Qatari Air Force One:
When journalists asked why they were told to shut their window shades while leaving Turkey, Trump admitted it was a risky flight. “You’re, you know, probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with,” he said.
But when asked if there was a credible threat to Air Force One, Trump made a quip about the broad danger of flying with the president.
“I’m number one on their list, before you,” he said. “But if I go, you go, right? So perhaps someday you wanna change professions.”
Turns out it was more like, “If you go, I’ll be safe on some other Air Force plane.”

sources.news_title: President Trump used elaborate ruse to fly out of Turkey following summit because of Iran threat, report says
sources.text:
President Donald Trump secretly flew out of last month’s NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on an alternate military aircraft while the White House made it appear that the Republican president was flying on Air Force One, according to a report published by The Washington Post.
The Post said Monday the operation was prompted by an Iranian assassination threat against Trump. The ruse was carried out as journalists and some White House staff members were led to believe they were on the same plane as the president as he began his journey back to Washington from the annual gathering of NATO country leaders.
The Post cited material reviewed by the newspaper, a U.S. official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the president’s travel. The Associated Press has not independently confirmed the report.
Trump had flown to the summit in a new Qatari-gifted and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet. But ahead of departing Turkey, he said he would fly partway home on an older-model baby blue Air Force One plane instead.
The president at the time said the new luxury jet was being flown out ahead of his departure from Ankara to give some U.S. troops based in eastern England a chance to check out the new Air Force One.
In Ankara, Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras ahead of the plane flying to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in the United Kingdom.
However, according to the Post report, after boarding the legacy Air Force One jet, he was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane — an Air Force C-32A — via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies. Trump flew to Mildenhall on that smaller jet.
The White House did not respond directly to questions about the Post report of the secret operation to whisk Trump out of the country on a third aircraft, or the reported elaborate ruse to make it appear he was on the baby blue Air Force One jet flying to Mildenhall.
“As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
The U.S. Secret Service declined to comment. The Air Force, which maintains the fleet of executive travel aircraft, referred questions to the White House.
There have been questions about the safety of the new Qatari-gifted plane
While Trump was in Turkey, the U.S. military conducted a series of large strikes in Iran in retaliation for its attacks on merchant shipping in the region.
The New York Times and CBS News reported last month that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a potential attack on the president or his jet, triggering additional precautions and the decision not to use the newly inaugurated aircraft gifted to Trump by Qatar for the first leg of Trump’s trip home from Ankara.
The swap had spurred questions about the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft, and Trump said last month after the trip that it would undergo additional upgrades.
Cheung on Monday maintained that the new, Qatari-gifted plane was “a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff.”
The new Post report on clandestinely putting Trump on a third aircraft and quietly whisking him out of the country adds a fresh layer to just how seriously concerned U.S. security officials were about the threat against Trump during the ongoing war with Iran.
Paul Eckloff, a former special agent with the Secret Service, said such an unusual move could either reflect actionable intelligence or an abundance of caution given volatility in the region with the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
“I would not say unprecedented, but it is an unusual occurrence,” Eckloff told The Associated Press.
The Post reported that to exit that plane without being seen by those uninvolved in the operation, Trump and several aides stepped aboard an airport catering truck, which was elevated planeside using hydraulics and positioned at a door on the opposite side of Air Force One’s entrance.
The small group of reporters who thought they were traveling with Trump were advised to lower their window shades ahead of takeoff.
After arriving at Mildenhall, news photographers captured images of Trump getting off the presidential plane — suggesting he reboarded Air Force One out of sight of the pack of journalists who thought they were traveling with him.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal called for a congressional briefing on what happened.
“It is unprecedented and it is surreal,” he said Monday on CNN, calling the incident “downright scary.”
After the brief visit to the base at Mildenhall, Trump boarded the new Air Force One aircraft to fly the rest of the way to Washington.
During a gaggle with reporters aboard the aircraft, Trump was asked directly if there was any credible threats on Air Force One by Iran.
“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” Trump said. He added to the traveling reporters, “But if I go, you go.”

sources.news_title: President Donald Trump Allegedly Hid in Catering Truck to Sneak Out of Turkey After Iranian Threat
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s recent exit out of Turkey was allegedly much more than just an ordinary travel day.
According to multiple reports, Trump, 80, secretly slipped out of Turkey in July on an alternate military plane, which he boarded while hidden inside a catering truck. (The White House previously stated he was aboard Air Force One.)
The security plan — first reported by The Washington Post — showcased the lengths officials went to in order to protect Trump from being assassinated by Iran.
The mission was carried out unbeknownst to journalists and even some White House staff members, who believed they were on the same plane as the president, according to The Washington Post.
Trump himself confirmed via social media in July that he would use the “former Air Force One” to fly out of Turkey. (He flew to the country on a new plane gifted by Qatar and meant to be used as Air Force One.)
“To honor our brave men and women of the Military, we are sending the brand new, and truly spectacular, Air Force One to Mildenhall Air Force Base, in the United Kingdom, to give them a chance to tour the Aircraft — Everybody is so excited, and we thought that they should be the first,” he wrote via Truth Social on July 8. “For old time’s sake, we’ll be taking the former Air Force One, from Turkey to Mildenhall, a short trip that is totally worth doing in order to give our Great Military Heroes a chance to appreciate our beautiful new addition to the Air Force Fleet!”
Us has reached out to the White House for comment.
When asked about the reports of a secret plane switch, White House spokesperson Steven Cheung told CNN, “The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff. As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
Trump was in Ankara for a NATO summit with various world leaders. The operation occurred one evening after United States forces renewed military strikes on Iran at Trump’s direction following a breakdown of peace negotiations.
The military conflict between the U.S. and Iran continues to focus heavily on economic warfare and control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
According to officials, 18 U.S. service members have died in the war with Iran since military operations began on February 28.

sources.text:
Donald Trump Reportedly Hid in Airport Food Truck Amid ‘Credible’ Iranian Assassination Threat, Air Force One Used as Decoy
President Donald Trump hid in a food truck amid an assassination threat, according to a new report.
The 80-year-old President of the United States hid in an airport catering truck to secretly fly out of Turkey on a military jet, according to a new report from The Washington Post.
The White House has said publicly that he was aboard Air Force One when he left the NATO summit in Ankara back in July.
Why Was Donald Trump Allegedly Hidden in an Airport Catering Truck?
The report claims that an Iranian assassination threat against President Trump resulted in the “extraordinary operation.”
Air Force One Was Reportedly Used as a Decoy
According to an anonymous U.S. official and other materials reviewed by the outlet, Trump was seen on TV boarding the old Air Force One jumbo jet before being “secretly shuttled” to a smaller plane (Air Force C-32A) “via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight,” making Air Force One a “decoy” with media and some White House staffers on the plane.
White House Responds to Report About Trump’s Security
White House communications director Steven Cheung issued a statement in response.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff. As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
A “credible threat” to Trump involving Iran led to the “deception operation,” per the U.S. official. For more details about the alleged operation, head to the Washington Post.
Trump just recently admitted to “error” regarding the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool amid claims of vandalism.

sources.text:
Okay, the part to be angry about is that he used some of his own staff and some people in my business to save his own desiccated hide.
An Iranian assassination threat against President Donald Trump prompted an extraordinary operation last month in which he flew secretly from Turkey on an alternate military aircraft while the White House said he was aboard Air Force One, The Washington Post has learned.
The clandestine mission, which has not been reported previously, was carried out unbeknownst to journalists and some White House staff members who believed they were on the same plane as the president, according to material reviewed by The Post, a U.S. official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the president’s travel. These people spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk about the matter.
What a reckless, overboiling pot of molten sociopathy this man is.
Now, back to the comedy.

In Ankara, Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras. He was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane—an Air Force C-32A—via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, according to the U.S. official and corroborating material reviewed by The Post. That made Air Force One a “decoy” with media and some White House staff aboard, the official said.
President Lincoln came to Washington on a heavily fortified train disguised by a wool hat instead of his trademark stovepipe. President Trump came back to Washington disguised as a load of Bud Light.

And, of course, much of the entire comic opera can be attributed to the Super Cool Jet Aeroplane—Bribe Force One—gifted to the president by the oil sheikhs of Qatar. This gaudy lemon had to be retooled so that some kid in Maine couldn’t accidentally pick up national-security discussions on his laptop. Once again, the lies point the way.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff,” Cheung’s statement said. “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
Including, apparently, state-of-the-art, high-level-security booze carts. There are many ways to fight a war. Some of them are stranger than others.

sources.news_title: Trump said to have secretly used military jet to leave Turkey amid threats | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Trump said to have secretly used military jet to leave Turkey amid threats
Top administration officials engaged in an elaborate deception to spirit President Donald Trump out of Turkey during the NATO summit there last month, transporting him in a catering container to a military jet because of a threat against him and Air Force One from Iran, two senior U.S. officials said Monday.
Trump and other officials had said publicly that he would be leaving Turkey on July 8 aboard one of the older versions of Air Force One rather than a luxury 747-8 donated by Qatar that he had flown in on. Trump told reporters at the time that he was making the switch for “old time’s sake.”
Trump boarded the older plane from the left-side door in view of cameras and news organizations, including The New York Times, reported that he had traveled on it to Britain, where he switched back to the newer plane. The Times reported at the time that the decision was driven in part by concern about the security of the new plane donated by Qatar, which had not been equipped with all the defensive capabilities of older versions.
But instead of flying out aboard that older, powder blue, modified 747, Trump was whisked off that plane via a catering container that had been lifted to the opposite side of the plane from where the journalists traveling with him boarded, one of the U.S. officials said. The president was then taken to a third plane, which he flew in secret to Britain, the official with knowledge of the matter said.
Reporters on the older plane were not told that Trump had not flown with them from Turkey to an air base in Britain, making them unwitting participants in the ruse and leaving them, along with some White House staff members, to serve as unknowing decoys.
After Trump arrived in Britain, he was secretly moved back to the older version of Air Force One. He then disembarked in view of reporters and walked across the tarmac to the plane donated by Qatar, which he flew to Washington.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
The elaborate plan appears to have been developed in a matter of hours after officials determined that a threat against Trump from Iran was credible. It came after years of threats against Trump from Iran and amid the war he launched against that country. And it was an unusual instance of the public being deceived about a president’s whereabouts.
Officials have not previously acknowledged that Trump was not where they claimed he was. The furtive operation was reported earlier by the Washington Post, which identified the plane that carried the president to Britain from Turkey as a C-32A, a military variant of a Boeing 757.
It is rare for presidents to travel without the reporters who comprise the press pool designated to be with them or in their vicinity, without those reporters having some general awareness of the commander in chief’s whereabouts.
President George W. Bush kept a slimmed-down press pool with him as he flew first to a military base and then back to Washington in the chaotic hours after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. And presidents — including Trump — have traveled to war zones with reporters alongside them.
Donald Mihalek, a former Secret Service agent who worked in the protective details for Bush and President Barack Obama, said the Secret Service has used decoy motorcades and flights in the past to move presidents secretly.
“Any time the president is in a theater where there’s potential combat danger, the Secret Service has employed protective countermeasures including the use of a decoy,” Mihalek said.
He added that the agency has long prioritized the security of the president over transparency with the public.
“The agency is not the agency of public affairs,” he said. “The agency is the agency of the Secret Service. Their No. 1 job is to keep the president safe.”
In this case, the threat led the White House to purposely mislead reporters assigned to cover Trump, leaving journalists to report that he was traveling on board a plane that was being used as a decoy.
After the Times reported last month on the security shortcomings of the Qatari-donated jet amid the concerns about the threat from Iran, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, seemed to hint that subterfuge might have been involved in Trump’s departure from Turkey.
“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal — including distraction and misdirection — to address those threats,” he said at the time.
The threat from Iran was not specific to the Qatari-donated jet, people familiar with the sequence of events said. Instead, Trump was being targeted on whatever airplane he was traveling on, as the Times has previously reported.
Trump was briefed on the threat while in Turkey, and a plan was soon put in place, with a small group of top government officials involved, including Gen. Dan Caine, the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to the official with knowledge of the deception plan.
The Defense Department and a spokesperson for Caine referred all questions to the White House on Monday. The White House reissued Cheung’s statement from the week of the NATO summit, only without the clause mentioning “distraction and misdirection.” The U.S. officials with knowledge of the deception plan spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security issues.
When Trump arrived at the airport to leave Turkey, a camera that had been positioned beforehand captured him getting on the old Air Force One, and journalists traveling with him, rushing to board the plane through lower steps in the back, had only a glimpse of him. A pool report noted as the plane took off, “We have been advised to keep our window shades in the press cabin closed.”
The older Air Force One landed at 10:16 p.m. at the Mildenhall military base in England, a pool report said, with Trump stepping off it 40 minutes later. Before that, unbeknown to reporters, Trump was brought by vehicle from the third plane that he had arrived on to the older Air Force One, boarded it through a different entrance and strode down the step from the upper left-side door as he would typically do, according to the U.S. official.
He walked from there to the Qatari jet, as the small group of reporters who had traveled aboard the older jet watched. The president and the press pool then boarded the new plane to fly back to Washington.
When asked by reporters during that flight back to the United States about why they had flown on the old Air Force One to England, Trump claimed he had wanted the troops stationed at the U.K. base to see the new plane. When pressed on why the window blinds had been directed to be shut on the flight from Turkey, Trump said that he knew of no specific threat but described himself as under constant siege from Iran.
“I’m No. 1 on their list, before you,” he told the reporters. “But if I go, you go. Right?
Trump and a number of his advisers have faced threats from Iran for years, especially after Trump, during his first term, ordered the killing of a powerful Iranian commander, Maj. Gen. Qassem Soleimani.
Trump’s advisers during the 2024 campaign privately told allies that they were given intelligence that Iran still hoped to harm Trump. That led to the occasional use of decoy planes during the campaign. His staff at times put the candidate aboard a secret jet, without alerting the media, while his staff flew his private plane. The Biden administration increased security for Trump that summer after new intelligence about plots to kill Trump; a short time later, he faced an unrelated assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, at an outdoor rally. There was a second unrelated attempt in September 2024.
The collective threats, which ranged from a prosecuted murder-for-hire plot by an Iranian proxy to the hacking of Trump campaign officials’ email and social media accounts, created a siege climate for the candidate and his aides. It led to fear, insularity and, at times, paranoia, that shaped how officials interacted with the Biden administration, which was responsible for allocating Secret Service resources, as well as with the media, and with other government officials.
After the Times reported about the security concerns in Turkey, and the fact that the Qatari jet lacked the same defensive capabilities as the older presidential aircraft, Trump was enraged by the leaks. The Justice Department issued subpoenas for grand jury testimony to the reporters who had been on the bylines of the stories, as well as some of their family members. Those subpoenas were withdrawn after a federal judge admonished federal prosecutors for the process involved.
Trump has continued to rage about information coming from his government that contradicts what he is telling the public, particularly about the war in Iran that he began Feb. 28, according to multiple officials.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

sources.news_title: Trump took a secret flight out of Turkey in an elaborate plot to hide his location amid Iran war
sources.text:
President Donald Trump was whisked out of Turkey last month on a military aircraft in an elaborate plot to keep his location secret amid security fears from the war with neighboring Iran, according to a U.S. official with knowledge of the plan.
The Washington Post was first to report the details of the clandestine operation, which included using a catering truck to get the president on the C-32 that flew from Ankara to the Mildenhall air force base in the United Kingdom.
The U.S. official confirmed the accuracy of these details. Trump deplaned the C-32, again secretly, and reboarded the older Air Force One jet to emerge in public view of cameras to eventually walk across the tarmac to the newer Qatari-donated jet, which lacks certain security measures and will soon be further retrofitted.
When reached for comment Monday night, White House communications director Steven Cheung did not dispute the Post’s story, which cited material reviewed by the Post, a U.S. official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the president’s travel.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff,” he said. “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
He provided a similar statement in July when asked why Trump flew on an older Air Force One instead of the newer one gifted by Qatar between Ankara and Mildenhall, and noted at the time that “distraction and misdirection” are some of the tools at the government’s disposal. The most recent statement did not include that phrase.
In both statements, Cheung said: “The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff.”
The White House on Monday also shared a statement from the U.S. Air Force about the new Air Force One that Trump decided not to fly on as he left Turkey.
“The aircraft is safe, secure and equipped with the most advanced technologies necessary to meet the requirements of the presidential mission,” the Air Force said.
The Secret Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night.
Senate Democrats want a briefing on exactly what happened.
“The Senate should be immediately briefed on the Iranian threats against the President, the extraordinary measures taken to get him out of Turkey, any risks posed to U.S. personnel, and any threat to the homeland,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said in a statement Tuesday, adding it was “unacceptable that Congress was kept in the dark” and learned about the mission through news reports.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on Monday night called Trump’s undisclosed travels “downright scary.”
“There has to be a congressional briefing because it involves not just the safety of the president,” he said during an interview with CNN. “I want to know what precautions were taken to make sure that all of the passengers on that Air Force One, which was judged too dangerous for the president to fly on, what precautions were taken to keep the staff and reporters on that plane safe.”
Trump announced on the morning of July 8 that he would take the “former Air Force One” from Turkey to the U.K. “for old time’s sake.” He said the new Qatari-gifted plane would be taken separately to Mildenhall air base in Britain to give troops a chance to see the new jet.
That evening, Trump boarded the old Air Force One in Ankara in front of TV cameras.
As the events of the secret mission unfolded, journalists who usually travel with the president, already on board the old Air Force One, were instructed to lower their window shades, according to a press pool report from that day.
When speaking to reporters during the flight from Britain to the United States on the Qatari-gifted plane, Trump was asked why journalists had been instructed to close their blinds, a detail the reporter asking the question called “weird.”
“You’re probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with,” Trump said.
Asked at the time if he was aware of a credible threat against him from Iran, Trump said he has “a threat all the time.”
“I’m No. 1 on their list, before you. But if I go, you go, right?” Trump told reporters. “Perhaps someday you want to change professions.”
He also denied that there were security issues with the new Air Force One plane that could have prompted him to switch aircraft in Turkey.
The U.S. government has undertaken decoy missions to protect U.S. presidents before, but their whereabouts were later revealed to the public.
In the hours after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, the White House told reporters that President George W. Bush was taken to an “undisclosed location,” later revealing he had been taken to a military facility in Nebraska. The year before, when President Bill Clinton visited Pakistan, he descended from an unmarked white plane that had followed Air Force One. His exit, in plain sight, revealed that Clinton had not been on the presidential aircraft.
Footage from July 8 captured by the broadcast press pool shows an airport catering truck pulling up to the side of Air Force One after Trump boarded in Ankara, moments before staff and journalists loaded the same aircraft.
The catering truck pulled away from Air Force One about five minutes after Trump boarded, driving toward the C-32A plane. The truck was parked near the back for four minutes before pulling away.
A press pool note later that day said the flight from Ankara to Mildenhall had been “uneventful,” adding that Trump had not visited the press cabin as he sometimes does. The president was seen deplaning from the jet in Britain, meaning he would have had to sneak back on board Air Force One once at Mildenhall.
NBC News previously reported that a security decision led Trump to take the old Air Force One out of Ankara, a day after the ceasefire with Iran came to an end. The Secret Service urged Trump to fly on the old jet, sources told NBC News in July. The decision was made in consultation with the White House Military Office and the Defense Department. The new plane from Qatar, the sources said, did not have all the security measures that the old one did.
Trump said some days later that the Qatari-gifted plane would be sent away to get “maxed out” for upgrades. That plane, a $400 million Boeing 747, prompted controversy when it was given to him by the Qatari government.
Trump maintained that it would be displayed at his new presidential library in Miami. But last week, the president’s son Eric Trump told NBC News that a different Air Force One will be displayed in the museum, leaving the Qatari plane’s fate uncertain.

sources.news_title: Trump 'hid in catering truck, sneaked into military jet' from Turkey amid Iran threat
sources.text:
Trump 'hid in catering truck, sneaked into military jet' from Turkey amid Iran threat
Mail This Article
Washington: U.S. President Donald Trump took a secret military flight from Turkey last month in an operation that involved him being moved between aircraft in a catering truck, an extraordinary deception prompted by an Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported.
The White House said at the time that the president was flying aboard Air Force One from Turkey, where he had attended a NATO summit, to Britain. But moments after Trump had boarded the plane, he left it in secret via the catering truck and boarded another aircraft for the flight to Britain, the Post said on Monday, quoting unnamed sources.
The New York Times carried a similar report, quoting unnamed U.S. officials.
Trump had taken a newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but unexpectedly announced he would use an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.
The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkey.
Before departing Ankara, Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" to RAF Mildenhall in Britain while the new plane stopped at the same base so U.S. service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.
After Trump boarded the old Air Force One in front of cameras in Ankara, he was secretly shuttled by the airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Post reported citing a U.S. official familiar with the operation and corroborating material it reviewed.
Secret switch
The deception operation was triggered by a credible threat to Trump, the Post reported. A similar operation had taken place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.
On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were traveling with Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed. The Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.
When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight". He went on to say: “But if I go, you go. Right?"
The C-32A carrying Trump flew to Britain and arrived at around 10:20 p.m. with the older Air Force One and media arriving minutes later, the Post reported. It was not clear, the paper said, how Trump was moved from the C-32A back to the older Air Force One.
Trump's traveling press pool reported he climbed down the stairs of the older Air Force One at 10:56 p.m. He gave the press a peace sign but didn't walk over to talk to them. He then spent some time greeting service members before walking to the new, Qatar-donated plane.
When asked for comment on the revelation of a secret flight on a third plane, the White House provided a statement from Communications Director Steve Cheung saying the Qatari-donated jet has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.
"As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," Cheung said. It was the same statement provided to the Post.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The new plane, with red, white, dark blue and gold livery chosen by Trump, is a Boeing 747 gifted to the United States by Qatar last year and refitted by defense contractor L3Harris Technologies. It was intended to serve as a temporary replacement while Boeing struggled to deliver long-delayed next-generation Air Force One planes.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump 'hid in catering cart' amid assassination threat
sources.text:
American president Donald Trump is reported to have flown out of Turkey last month on a decoy plane amid a recent assassination threat.
The US leader attended the Nato summit in Turkey, but departed the city on an alternative military aircraft.
This came as White House officials made it appear that the president was flying on Air Force One.
The Washington Post reported the decoy, detailing that the operation was spurred by an Iranian assassination threat.
The publication was informed of the mission by a US official.
The 80-year-old American had arrived in Turkey in a new Qatar-gifted, retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet.
He had said he would be flying back to the States on an older baby blue-coloured Air Force One plane.
On his departure from Ankara, Trump was seen boarding said plane.
The report from the Post revealed, however, that Trump was secretly transferred to a smaller plane just minutes later.
The president was shuttled onto the Air Force C-32A via an airport catering truck, usually used to load meals and other supplies.
Trump was scheduled to fly to Mildenhall, and did so on the smaller jet.
A statement from White House communications director Steven Cheung told the publication: ‘As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.’

sources.news_title: Trump Uses Press Corps as Decoy to Evade Iran Threat
sources.text:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.
Air Force None
By now, you’ve likely ingested many of the details from the bombshell Washinton Post report on the elaborate security operation and public misinformation campaign to spirit President Trump out of Ankara, Turkey, following last month’s NATO summit in order to avoid a credible threat to his life from Iran.
The entire ruse is remarkable by the historic standards of security theater and continuity of government protocols that have hovered over our political consciousness since the peak tensions of the Cold War nuclear standoff with the Soviet Union.
Especially striking is that White House staff and the press pool who remained on the older model Air Force One that everyone thought Trump was aboard ended up serving as decoys — sitting ducks for whatever scheme Iran had conjured up but ultimately failed in or decided not to execute.
The image we conjure in our minds of Trump boarding Air Force One on one side of the plane before secretly exiting the other side into a waiting catering truck is indelible. But I’m just as taken by what happened after Trump’s secret flight landed in the U.K.
Once on the ground, Trump had to be secretly returned to the older Air Force One, then make a show of disembarking from it before boarding the new Qatari Force One that he took across the Atlantic to Joint Base Andrews. As you may know, the Air Force One call sign only applies when the president is aboard the aircraft, but I’m taking some liberties with the term here for the sake of clarity.
“It’s not clear how Trump moved from the C-32A to the legacy Air Force One after landing,” the WaPo noted.
The NYT has a more robust account of this part of the operation: “Before that, unbeknown to reporters, Mr. Trump was brought by vehicle from the third plane that he had arrived on to the older Air Force One, boarded it through a different entrance and strode down the step from the upper left-side door as he would typically do, according to the U.S. official.”
Here is he pretending to have just flown in on the older Air Force One:
Here he is walking between the old and new Air Force One aircraft:
This entire episode would be notable in its own right, but the NYT’s subsequent reporting on the ostensible version of what happened — the old Air Force One was used because the new Qatari-gifted one lacked sufficient defense capabilities given the Iranian threat — gave rise to a leak investigation and highly controversial subpoenas to NYT reporters.
Those subpoenas have since been withdrawn, but it’s a bit of a mindfuck to try to piece together that related saga in light of this new information. Was the administration, for instance, agitated not just that the new Air Force One was being denigrated by the NYT’s reporting but that the NYT was onto the secret mission to extricate Trump from Turkey? We don’t know if the NYT had additional information on the ruse that it didn’t publish, though its followup to yesterday’s WaPo exclusive didn’t betray any previous unpublished knowledge of the operation.
The Corruption: Trump DOJ Edition
U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis sharply criticized principal associate deputy attorney general Trent McCotter in dropping criminal fraud charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani and several of his co-defendants.
Judge Garaufis largely (but not entirely) granted the Trump DOJ’s motion to dismiss the case, but, in a withering 47-page order, he shellacked political appointee McCotter for pushing the dismissal through without consultation with investigators:
On the current record, McCotter appears to have eschewed the professional opinions of innumerable officials from various federal offices and replaced them with his singular judgment. The fact that McCotter came to this decision largely in collaboration with defense counsel, and seemingly without input from the FBI and SEC agents who investigated the alleged misconduct, or the attorneys from the Department, SEC, and U.S. Attorney’s Office who brought the case, appears to be highly unusual.
Garaufis also flamed McCotter for claiming the indictment was the handiwork of a politicized Biden DOJ:
McCotter appears to be accusing officials across four different government offices of bringing a detailed 54-page, 5-count indictment out of spite. However, he has not provided a scintilla of evidence to suggest that the timing of the unsealing of the indictment, or the charging decisions, in this case was politically motivated. McCotter’s baseless assertion is unbecoming of his office.
The dismissal of the case against Adani, essentially a foreign bribery case of the kind that the Trump DOJ has de-emphasized pursuing, came after Adani retained Bob Giuffra and Jamie McDonald (who Trump later nominated as Manhattan U.S. attorney) of Sullivan & Cromwell (which is representing Trump personally in other matters). In a presentation to McCotter at the Justice Department, Giuffra reportedly said that Adani would be willing to invest $10 billion in the American economy if the charges were dropped, according to CBS News.
Trump DOJ Watch
- ICYMI: The Southern Poverty Law Center’s motion for vindictive prosecution was denied Friday by the trial judge, who declined to look past federal prosecutors in Alabama to Main Justice or to the White House in assessing improper motives for bringing the politicized case.
- Reflecting Pool: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) will make an effort to extract information from the Trump DOJ about the charging decision in the since-dismissed Reflecting Pool case against David Hearn, Greg Sargent reports.
- OLC Dramatically Expands Claimed Scope of Executive Privilege: The president can assert executive privilege over communications with “private advisers … so long as they relate to official presidential decisionmaking, involve or reflect communications with the President or his direct advisers, and are confidential,” the Office of Legal Counsel asserts in a new memo flagged by Punchbowl.
Photo of the Day

- Politico: Families, lawyers and judges describe a year of frantic emergency cases after a Trump administration memo reversed decades of interpretation of federal law and allowed ICE to begin detaining without bond hearings people who have lived in the U.S. for years. Federal judges have since ruled against the Trump detention policy more than 16,000 times.

Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, writing about President Trump’s new birthright citizenship executive orders:
The Citizenship Clause was indeed written to repudiate Dred Scott, the 1857 Supreme Court decision holding that Black people could never be citizens. But the Reconstruction Congress did not swap one caste rule for a narrower one; it extended the promise to “every free-born person in this land.” The idea wasn’t just to retroactively protect “the babies of slaves”; it was to prospectively forestall all future efforts to deny citizenship based on whatever other non-sovereignty-based criteria might be politically popular in any given moment.

sources.text:
Report: Trump left plane in cart to thwart Iran plot
Reporters flying with Trump were not told he wasn’t on board
What happened
President Donald Trump left a NATO summit in Turkey last month aboard an alternate military aircraft after publicly boarding Air Force One, then secretly exiting from the plane’s opposite side in an “airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight,” The Washington Post reported Monday, citing U.S. officials and “corroborating material.” The “elaborate deception” to “spirit” Trump out of the region was prompted by a credible “threat against him and Air Force One from Iran,” The New York Times said.
Who said what
The “furtive operation” was apparently “developed in a matter of hours,” the Times said. Reporters flying with Trump were not told of the deception, thereby “making them unwitting participants in the ruse and leaving them, along with some White House staff members, to serve as unknowing decoys.” The journalists and staffers were not “made aware of the extent of the threat on Air Force One,” the Post said.
When reporters asked Trump later why they had been advised to keep their window shades closed on the flight from Ankara to Britain, he said they were “probably on a dangerous flight,” but since he’s Iran’s top target, “if I go, you go.”

sources.news_title: BREAKING: Trump Evaded Iranian Assassination Plot With Split-Second Maneuver
sources.text:
Politics
BREAKING: Trump Evaded Iranian Assassination Plot With Split-Second Maneuver
President Donald Trump was secretly moved off Air Force One and onto a smaller military jet last month after U.S. officials received what they believed was a credible Iranian threat against his life, according to a bombshell new report.
The extraordinary deception operation unfolded July 8 as Trump prepared to leave Turkey following a NATO summit and renewed U.S. military strikes against Iran.
Trump initially boarded the familiar blue-and-white Air Force One in full view of television cameras at Ankara Esenboga Airport.
But minutes later, the president and several aides were reportedly moved out of sight through an airport catering truck and transferred to a nearby Air Force C-32A, a modified Boeing 757 commonly used to transport senior government officials.
The legacy Air Force One then departed carrying journalists and some White House staff who reportedly believed Trump was still aboard.
In reality, the president was flying separately under a low-profile military call sign as part of an elaborate security operation designed to conceal his location.
A U.S. official familiar with the mission described the larger aircraft as a “decoy.”
The maneuver came after intelligence officials identified a credible threat involving Iran, according to the report.
Trump had spent the previous day meeting NATO leaders in Ankara. The operation took place just one night after U.S. forces renewed strikes against Iran at his direction following the collapse of negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
🚨 UPDATE: Footage RELEASED of President Trump reportedly out-maneuvering an Iranian assassination plot in Turkey — hauled off in an airport catering truck from Air Force One, unbeknownst to the press — then he boarded the C-32A
Basically EVERYONE thought 47 was on the… pic.twitter.com/QpoDxGCNfq
— Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) August 11, 2026
The president’s real location remained hidden from much of the public and even some senior officials for hours.
White House communications director Steven Cheung defended the security measures surrounding presidential travel.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff,” Cheung’s statement said. “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
The threat reportedly involved concerns that Iran or its proxies could target Trump or his aircraft while he was leaving Turkey.
Those fears have intensified following years of Iranian threats against American officials, particularly after the United States killed senior Iranian military leaders and later became directly involved in the current conflict.
Turkey shares a border with Iran, adding another layer of concern for U.S. security officials.
The operation began after Trump publicly announced that he would leave Turkey aboard the “former Air Force One” rather than the newer Boeing 747-8 that had been gifted to the United States by Qatar.

That newer aircraft had recently undergone hundreds of millions of dollars in upgrades but reportedly lacked some of the defensive countermeasures found on the older presidential jets.
Trump boarded the legacy Air Force One at dusk and waved toward cameras on the tarmac.
According to the report, he then left the aircraft through a door on the opposite side using a catering truck typically used to load food and supplies.
The truck’s container was raised hydraulically to the plane’s door, allowing Trump and several aides to enter without being seen by reporters or others outside the operation.
The vehicle then drove toward the nearby C-32A.
Media footage reportedly showed the catering truck positioned beside the smaller military plane for several minutes before lowering again.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth separately boarded the C-32A using exterior stairs in what was reportedly designed to make the flight appear routine.
Trump and Hegseth then flew to Britain aboard the smaller aircraft.
Meanwhile, White House reporters boarding the decoy Air Force One were instructed to close their window shades.
The C-32A reportedly operated under the nondescript call sign “Reach 18” or “RCH18,” rather than the traditional Air Force One designation.
Tracking systems that normally allow the aircraft to be easily followed were also reportedly disabled.
The former Qatari aircraft flew separately to Britain’s RAF Mildenhall under the call sign “SAM 33,” while the legacy Air Force One carrying staff and journalists later began using “AF1” despite Trump not being aboard.
The three aircraft ultimately arrived in Britain within hours of one another.
RELATED: NEW: Feds Thwart Trump Assassination Plot At His LA Golf Club
Trump later appeared before television cameras descending from the legacy Air Force One, though it remains unclear exactly how he was transferred back onto that plane after landing.
He then boarded the newer presidential jet for the flight back to Washington.
During that flight, Donald Trump spoke with reporters about the continuing threat posed by Iran but did not reveal the elaborate deception operation that had just been carried out.
Asked why journalists had been ordered to lower their window shades in Turkey, Trump gave a characteristically blunt answer.
“because you’re probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with.”
RELATED: NEW: Plot To Assassinate Trump Exposed
Trump said that he has a “threat all the time” against his life and that he is “number one” on Iran’s “list.”
He then delivered a dark joke to the reporters traveling with him.
“But if I go, you go. Right?” Trump suggested to reporters. “Perhaps someday you want to change professions.”
Former acting Secret Service Director Ronald L. Rowe Jr. said keeping the methods used to protect a president hidden is critical.
“We need to keep the ‘secret’ in Secret Service,” said Rowe, now with the Chertoff Group, a security advisory firm. “The public should know what the president is doing on a daily basis, but when it comes to the methods by which the Secret Service keeps the president safe, that should remain out of public view.”
The White House and Pentagon have not publicly detailed the full scope of the threat or how close officials believed Iran came to acting on it.
What is now clear is that security officials considered the danger serious enough to turn one Air Force One into a decoy, hide the president inside a catering truck and secretly fly him out of Turkey aboard a military jet while much of the world believed he was somewhere else.

sources.text:
USA
President Donald Trump secretly switched from Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara, according to The Washington Post, in an elaborate security operation reportedly prompted by an Iranian threat against him.
Trump was publicly seen boarding an older-model Air Force One at Ankara airport after the NATO summit, leading journalists and some White House staff to believe he would fly aboard the presidential jet to Britain.
But according to the Post, Trump was secretly transferred minutes later to a smaller Air Force C-32A.
The newspaper reported that Trump and several aides used an airport catering truck to move between aircraft without being seen by those outside the operation.
The Associated Press has not independently confirmed the report.
Reported threat prompts precautions
The operation was reportedly driven by concerns over a potential Iranian assassination attempt against Trump as the conflict between the United States and Iran intensified.
The New York Times and CBS News had previously reported that U.S. intelligence officials raised concerns about a possible attack against the president or his aircraft, prompting additional security measures.
The White House did not directly respond to questions about the reported aircraft switch. The Secret Service also declined to comment, while the Air Force referred questions to the White House.
Journalists kept in the dark
The operation was designed to make it appear that Trump remained aboard the older Air Force One jet.
A small group of reporters travelling with the president was instructed to lower window shades before takeoff.
Trump instead flew to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in Britain aboard the C-32A, while the legacy Air Force One aircraft continued on its publicly expected route.
Photographers at Mildenhall later captured Trump disembarking from the presidential aircraft, creating the impression that he had travelled aboard it from Ankara.
Qatar jet adds another layer
Trump had travelled to the NATO summit aboard a newly refurbished Boeing aircraft gifted by Qatar, which is intended to become a future Air Force One.
Ahead of his return journey, Trump said the new aircraft would be flown separately to allow U.S. troops stationed in eastern England to inspect it.
The aircraft was later used for the final leg of Trump’s journey from Mildenhall to Washington.
The Qatar-provided jet had already become a focus of security concerns following reports that intelligence officials had advised against using it for the first leg of the return journey.
Trump subsequently said the aircraft would undergo additional security upgrades.
Trump acknowledges ongoing threat
During the flight, Trump was asked whether there was a credible Iranian threat against Air Force One.
“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” Trump told reporters.
He then warned the journalists travelling with him: “But if I go, you go.”
The reported operation offers a rare glimpse into the extraordinary security measures surrounding presidential travel as Washington remains engaged in a confrontation with Tehran.

sources.news_title: Trump Used Catering Truck to Dodge Iran Assassination Plot
sources.text:
President Trump secretly slipped away from Air Force One using an airport catering truck and boarded an alternate military aircraft to leave Turkey last month, an elaborate security maneuver prompted by a credible Iranian threat to assassinate him, according to a Washington Post report confirmed by CNN and corroborated by multiple other outlets. The operation, which had not previously been disclosed, was carried out without the knowledge of most journalists traveling with the president and even some White House staff, who believed they were traveling on the same plane as Trump throughout the departure.
Trump had arrived in Ankara on July 8 for a NATO leaders summit aboard a newly retrofitted Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar and outfitted to serve as the primary Air Force One. Hours before his departure that evening, Trump announced he would instead leave Turkey aboard the older Air Force One jet, telling reporters the switch was "for old time's sake" and that U.S. forces stationed at a refueling stop in the United Kingdom would get a chance to inspect the newer plane. CBS News has separately reported that the Secret Service had recommended the older aircraft for security reasons. Television footage showed Trump walking up the stairs of the older jet in front of cameras and disappearing inside, with a catering truck visible parked on the opposite side of the aircraft.
According to the Post's account, based on materials it reviewed and interviews with a U.S. official and another person familiar with the operation, Trump did not remain aboard that plane. Minutes after boarding, he and a small team of aides were moved out of public view through a door on the far side of the jet using the catering truck, which had been raised by a hydraulic lift to the aircraft's exit. The truck was lowered and driven across the tarmac to a separate U.S. Air Force C-32A, a military variant of the Boeing 757, which then carried Trump to a refueling stop in the United Kingdom. Meanwhile, the traveling press pool and White House staff boarded the older 747 believing Trump was aboard; reporters were instructed to keep the window shades in the press cabin closed for takeoff, and that aircraft departed as a decoy roughly 17 minutes after Trump had first been seen boarding it, according to a pool report reviewed by CNN.
Asked at the time why the shades needed to be closed, Trump told reporters they were "probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with," a remark that in hindsight referred to the assassination threat rather than the older plane he was never actually aboard. Once the decoy jet and Trump's actual plane both reached the refueling stop at RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, Trump was secretly transferred back to the newer, Qatari-donated Air Force One for the remainder of the flight to Washington, completing a sequence in which the president flew on three different aircraft during a single return trip while the public record showed only one.
The threat driving the operation stemmed from intelligence Israel shared with the United States regarding an alleged specific Iranian plot to assassinate Trump, according to the Jerusalem Post's account of the Washington Post reporting. The clandestine switch took place the night after U.S. forces had resumed military strikes against Iran at Trump's direction, following the collapse of ceasefire negotiations between Washington and Tehran, a sequence that placed the president's departure from Turkey directly in the immediate aftermath of renewed American strikes on Iranian territory. Fox News' account of the same reporting noted that concern also extended to the newer Qatari-donated jet's defensive capabilities, which the report described as less proven than those of the older, long-serving Air Force One airframe.
The disclosure adds new detail to an assassination-threat storyline that has surfaced repeatedly around Trump since before he returned to office. The New York Times reported earlier this summer on security concerns tied to the new Air Force One, prompting the Justice Department to subpoena four Times reporters to testify before a federal grand jury over their coverage, a move CNN reported followed a meeting between FBI Director Kash Patel and White House officials and a phone call between Patel and Trump in which Trump was described as angry and embarrassed that the security concerns had become public. A forthcoming book about Trump's political rise has also described a separate episode from before his return to office, in which his campaign used a decoy plane owned by Steve Witkoff after law enforcement warned that Iran had positioned operatives in the U.S. with access to surface-to-air missiles as part of an earlier assassination plot, a concern that intensified after a Secret Service intervention in a separate incident at one of Trump's golf clubs in Florida.
Trump has periodically referenced the broader threat environment surrounding him without detailing specific operational measures like the Turkey switch, at one point describing himself as Iran's "No. 1" target amid renewed conflict with Tehran. Neither the White House nor the Secret Service has issued a detailed public statement addressing the specific sequence of events in Ankara, and the operation's disclosure came entirely through the Post's reporting rather than any official confirmation offered proactively by the administration.
The episode illustrates how directly the renewed U.S.-Iran conflict has intersected with the day-to-day mechanics of protecting the president, extending beyond the war's more visible fronts, the Strait of Hormuz standoff, the naval blockade, the exchange of strikes, into decisions about which aircraft carries the president on ordinary diplomatic travel. Whether the Secret Service and White House adopt similar decoy measures for future presidential travel amid the continuing war, and whether further details about the specific nature of the Iranian threat eventually become public, are likely to remain open questions given the administration's evident preference, reflected in the DOJ subpoenas over earlier related reporting, for keeping such security details out of public view.
