Almost 10 years since he first took office, it often feels like Donald Trump has lost his ability to surprise us. He says outrageous things on a daily basis, but we are inured to that. His family businesses grow rich while he’s in the White House, but what else is new? Even the US President falling asleep on camera in the Oval Office is starting to get old.
The Trump show has been going on for many seasons now, and most of its plot lines feel familiar – but now and then, something comes along to show that he hasn’t entirely lost his ability to shock.
On Tuesday evening, The Washington Post reported jaw-dropping details of how Trump flew from the Nato summit in Turkey to the UK last month – at a time when he faced a heightened security risk from groups linked to neighbouring Iran. US intelligence had reportedly received credible threats that there might be an attempt to shoot down the President’s plane.
Timeline of recent Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure
Ukraine has maintained near-daily attacks on Russian oil refineries, pumping stations and exports – targeting the lifeblood of Moscow’s war economy.
By some estimates, the campaign has knocked out a third of Russia’s oil processing capacity.
What you need to know
On 18 July, Kyiv ushered in a new era, targeting Wildberries warehouses – Russia’s equivalent to Amazon and one of the country’s largest companies.
For many Russians, the war now feels a lot closer to home, with social media filled with videos of explosions and business owners crying over their destroyed stock.
Kyiv has raised the stakes in recent weeks with dozens of attacks. The logic is to aggravate economic problems and harm public support for the war.
30 April – Ukraine said it hit one of Russia’s largest oil refineries more than 1,500 kilometres from the front line.
24 June – A strike on an electricity substation took out the power in the Russian-occupied city of Sevastopol.
4 July – Ukraine hit a major oil terminal in St Petersburg.
2 August – Kyiv said it hit an oil refinery and airfield 600 kilometres from the border in Saratov region.
3 August – A drone hit a Wildberries warehouse in one of a series of similar attacks on the company.
6 August – Ukraine hit two oil refineries, trying to reduce the profits of Russian oil.
astronomy
When and where to catch a glimpse of Perseid meteor shower
Just hours after the partial solar eclipse, Wednesday night will see stargazers treated to yet another astronomical event.
But what is the Perseid meteor shower and where can you see it best?
Everything you need to know
The Perseids are seen as streaks of bright meteors across the night sky. They are caused by debris from the Swift-Tuttle comet and are seen in the UK every summer.
Its peak nights are 12 and 13 August this year. Much of the UK will have clear skies overnight, with a new moon meaning the display should also be more visible.
Where best to see it
Try to go somewhere without light pollution, preferably away from cities.
Allow your eyes to adjust to the darkness and gaze up towards the widest clear expanse of sky.
You could see hundreds of “shooting stars”, with the best time between midnight and sunrise.
Areas of the Highlands, mid-Wales and rural Northumberland are often cited as having the least light pollution.
Why billionaire Lord Sugar has hit out at American Express
Lord Alan Sugar has called American Express “a bunch of idiots” after he was denied an increase on his credit limit.
The Apprentice star, 79, who has a reported net worth of £1.138bn, said he spoke to someone who was aware of his “financial status”, but it made no difference.
What is the row about?
Lord Sugar wrote on X to complain he had been on the phone with American Express for an hour, and eventually “my request was refused due to their system”.
Replying to some criticism in his comments, the entrepreneur responded: “I AM NOT MOANING JUST EXPOSING WHAT A BUNCH OF IDIOTS AMEX ARE.”
Some in Lord Sugar’s comments accused him of “trying to flaunt your status” after championing his modest background.
Lord Sugar was born in Hackney, east London, in 1947 and grew up in a council flat.
He left school at 16 and briefly worked in the civil service as a statistician.
He founded electronics company Amstrad at the age of 21 and found commercial success by mass-producing affordable consumer electronics.
Sugar began hosting reality competition show The Apprentice in 2005.
He sold his stake in Amstrad to BSkyB in 2007 for £125m.
His net worth is reportedly £1.138bn.
ECONOMY
The tax changes that could come in October’s Budget
As speculation rises over the Chancellor’s plans, experts believe the upcoming Budget could see another “smorgasbord” of small tax changes.
The fiscal rules mean additional borrowing is very unlikely, while there is little headroom for more spending.
Will taxes rise and by how much?
Economist Julian Jessop said: “It is highly likely that further tax increases will be announced in the Budget.” Leading economic forecaster Capital Economics suggests tax rises up to £25bn are possible.
Although there are hundreds of possible tax rises, here are some of the key ones that could affect you.
There has been speculation that the Government could end up cutting the size of the tax-free lump sum people can take from their pensions, which is either 25 per cent of the amount or £268,275 – whichever is lower.
Shah believes this is a “sacred cow” among middle England and won’t be touched, but that pension tax relief could be.
Jessop believes the Budget could target business sectors that Labour believes engage in “antisocial” activities.
To a degree, Andy Burnham has done this already, announcing a 20 per cent business rates cut for pubs, clubs, and small live music venues funded by reducing reliefs for stores perceived as causing social harm.
Capital Economics believes “sin taxes” on the likes of unhealthy food could raise £1bn and be a possibility.
Wealth taxes
Though this could fall within the scope of large tax overhauls, Burnham is being urged heavily to consider changes.
Compass, a cross-party campaign group headed by Neal Lawson, is fronting a new report which includes calls for wealth tax reform.
The report proposes a 2 per cent levy on net wealth above £10m, which it says would raise £24bn a year from around 22,000 people – just 0.03 per cent of the population.

The airport that has overtaken Heathrow as Europe’s busiest
Heathrow airport said “the case for expansion has never been clearer” after it lost its position as Europe’s busiest airport.
Everything we know
Heathrow has lost its claim to the busiest airport in Europe to Istanbul. Heathrow’s two runways are operating at capacity, but passenger numbers are thought to be down due to the US-Israeli war with Iran.
The airport used the drop in numbers as a new argument in its long-standing campaign for a third runway. Reacting to the news, it said “the case for expansion has never been clearer”.
The story in numbers
8.15 million
Heathrow saw just 7.86 million customers pass through it in July, compared to 8.15 million in Istanbul.
The London airport recorded 84.46 million total passengers in 2025.
1.5% dive
Heathrow’s July passenger total represented a 1.5 per cent decrease compared with the same month last year, whereas Istanbul saw a 2.3 per cent boost.
On Middle East routes alone, Heathrow passenger numbers were down 20 per cent compared to last year.

The GLP-1 medication will be available to buy privately with a prescription after approval by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).
Everything we know
Foundayo is a daily weight-loss pill from Eli Lilly, the makers of Mounjaro.
The UK has become the first European country to approve its use.

It can help people lose an average of 12 per cent of their body weight.
We do not yet know if the pills will be available on the NHS. It will be available on prescription for private patients.
Why is this significant?
A trial in May found orforglipron, the scientific name for the drug, could be used to help patients maintain weight loss after coming off GLP-1 jabs.
Dr Louis Aronne, an obesity expert at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York, hailed it as a “treatment for life”.

Clare, 32, says her job is busy and she has to schedule sex with her partner on weekends, or some afternoons twice a month. “Occasionally this slips and I do worry that it makes us not as connected,” she says.
Gen X

I haven’t had the issue of my sex life drying up with menopause. I’m more aroused now.

I did what I thought I was supposed to do and forgot my needs and wants. I think it’s really important that you’re an individual and not just a person who is married.
KATIE STRATFORD*, A 55-YEAR-OLD MUM OF TWO, WHO DIVORCED ATER 19 YEARS
Small things, like being brought a cup of tea or saying thank you, make a big difference.
Therapists

People don’t talk about the deep issues; nobody else is going to do it for you. You don’t want to ask questions because it might rock the boat…you have to keep talking, and talk about what it is that you want within the relationship to keep going forward.
KATIE STRATFORD
Seven rules to save your marriage
Remember that things change
“What you see on social media and what friends say is quite often the nice version. Everything is a phase,” says Deulofeu.
Look at yourself first
“Focus on what’s in your control and what you can do differently, rather than the other person or a situation that you can’t control. Invest in understanding yourself,” she adds.
After ostentatiously boarding Air Force One – waving to the camera as he did so – Trump was bundled into a catering truck and transferred to a different military plane. The entire operation was clandestine: “Air Force One” is usually the call sign for whatever plane the president is aboard, but in this case, Trump travelled as “Reach 18” instead.
The decision to move the President also means that Trump in effect used some of the USA’s most senior journalists as his human shields, or at least as decoys.
Trump or his security team decided it was too dangerous for the President to be on board Air Force One, but the unwitting group of reporters that accompanies Trump on overseas trips, known as the pool, believed they were flying on the same plane as the President.
The ruse was a staggeringly high-risk manoeuvre: Air Force One has some of the most advanced countermeasures against attack of any plane in the world. It is equipped as a mobile command centre for emergencies, and has security systems in place against attack that won’t have been present on the back-up aircraft.
At the time, Trump announced that he would be travelling on the “old” Air Force One instead of the brand new jet he had been personally gifted by Qatar, because of security concerns. Reports suggested US intelligence had received credible threats that there might be an attempt to shoot down the President’s plane.
This had been a source of embarrassment – Trump’s shiny new plane just didn’t have the same security measures as the decades-old jet the President so viscerally dislikes.
As it turns out, the President did not fly on the old Air Force One. Instead, Trump’s extraordinary decision to allow himself to be smuggled out of the plane in a catering truck meant that his White House operation lied to the world about the President’s location – something that, to public knowledge, hasn’t been done for decades. In the hours immediately after 9/11, the White House did not disclose George W Bush’s location, but it did not give false information about where he was. Trump broke with that precedent.
There might even have been a backfire risk: had an Iran-linked group chosen to use Trump’s visit to Turkey to launch an attack, they could have decided they would be unlikely to hit Air Force One itself successfully, and targeted a different, less protected plane travelling with it – only for it to be the one with Trump on board.
Whether the operation was the brainchild of Trump’s Secret Service protection detail, or that of an increasingly paranoid Trump, it was not without grave risk to the President – as well as the journalists and White House staff it used as decoys.
Trump has reasons to fear assassination, of course. In July 2024, he narrowly escaped an assassination attempt while speaking at a rally near Butler, Pennsylvania, during which a bullet seemingly grazed his ear. There have been several other attempts to target Trump since, including at his golf club in Florida in September 2024, and at the White House correspondents’ dinner this April, though none of these got anywhere close to the President.
The incident is an encapsulation of Trump’s second term. He was at risk due to a war against Iran he had launched, which he has repeatedly claimed was already won – even claiming to have agreed a peace deal. His new Air Force One, which will be owned by his presidential library for his personal use after he leaves the Oval Office, was not secure enough to use.
And so, to find a way out of this predicament entirely of Trump’s creation, someone conjured up a drastic plan that led to the President hiding with catering, turning journalists into human shields and breaking a decades-long precedent about not lying about the President’s whereabouts.
Trump’s fear of assassination might be well-grounded – but it is leading him into some very strange places indeed.

Trump used catering truck, decoy flight to avoid Iran threat as he flew out of Turkey: Report
The NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey last month, ended with a ruse to safely get President Trump out of the country due to Iranian assassination threats against him, according to The Washington Post.
Dig deeper:

The Post cited material reviewed by the newspaper, a U.S. official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the president’s travel. The Associated Press has not independently confirmed the report.
Trump had flown to the summit in a new Qatari-gifted and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet. But ahead of departing Turkey, he said he would fly partway home on an older-model baby blue Air Force One plane instead.
The president at the time said the new luxury jet was being flown out ahead of his departure from Ankara to give some U.S. troops based in eastern England a chance to check out the new Air Force One.
In Ankara, Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras ahead of the plane flying to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in the United Kingdom.
However, according to the Post report, after boarding the legacy Air Force One jet, he was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane — an Air Force C-32A — via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies. Trump flew to Mildenhall on that smaller jet.

sources.news_title: Iran Threat Prompted Trump To Secretly Swap Planes While Leaving Turkey, Reports Say
sources.text:
Topline
President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes last month and left Turkey on board a much smaller plane in response to a purported Iranian threat, according to multiple reports, the latest development involving Trump’s departure from the NATO summit and Air Force One.
Key Facts
According to the Washington Post, which first reported the story, the president boarded the older Air Force One jet as announced by the White House while leaving Turkey, but was then secretly taken to a much smaller plane.
Trump was taken to an Air Force Boeing C-32A plane—the type of jet primarily used by the vice president and other senior cabinet members—onboard an airport catering truck used to carry meals and other supplies.
Previous reporting about Trump’s departure from Turkey focused on him using the old Air Force One jet instead of the new Qatar-gifted one due to its purported lack of security features—but the Post reported that the old plane served as a “decoy” because of the swap.
The New York Times, which corroborated the report, noted that some White House staff members and the reporters on board the larger jet were not made aware of the secret swap and believed they were flying with the president on board.
After the planes landed in the U.K., Trump was secretly brought back on board the older plane that serves as Air Force One and disembarked in view of the reporters before switching over to the Qatar-gifted jet.
The president has not yet publicly commented on the latest reporting about the swap.
Chief Critic
Democratic Party consultant and former President Barack Obama’s ex-campaign adviser David Axelrod criticized the White House’s decision to use the old plane as a decoy with journalists on board. He told CNN, “Reporters understood that there are elements of that trip that needed to be kept under wraps until after the president was safely in and out of those places,” but noted that the American people deserve to know that the threat level was so high. He also added: “Everyone on that plane was a decoy. If they felt that it was unsafe to be on the plane, then it was unsafe for everybody else to be on the plane as well. So, they at least deserve to know…why this was happening.”
key background
The report about the jet swap comes weeks after concerns about the safety of the new Qatar-gifted jet first emerged as the Ankara trip served as its international debut as the new Air Force One. Trump flew on board the new plane to attend the NATO summit but the White House announced he would fly the first half of his return leg from Ankara to RAF Mildenhall, a U.S. Air Force base in the U.K., on board the old Air Force One. At the time the president and White House insisted that the switch was done to allow U.S. service members stationed at the base “a chance to tour the Aircraft,” however reports suggested that this was done at the request of the Secret Service amid a renewed conflict with Iran. After landing in the U.K., the president switched back over the new Qatari jet.
tangent
While flying on board the new Qatari jet, from RAF Mildenhall in the U.K. to Joint Base Andrews, Trump was asked if he was aware of “any credible threat by Iran to Air Force One.” At the time, the president told the reporter, “Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list, before you. But if I go, you go…Perhaps someday you want to change professions.” Trump’s suggestion that he reporters on board Air Force One faced the same threat as him is likely to draw some scrutiny after these reports that they were flying onboard what was effectively a decoy plane.
what do we know about planned upgrades to the Qatar Jet?
Later that month, Trump was asked again about reports of the the Qatari jet lacking certain defensive features like onboard antimissile defense systems. Trump said the plane is set to undergo another set of upgrades and to get its security capabilities “maxed out.” He claimed that the process would take only one month but did not specify what these “maxed out” upgrades would cover and its unclear if the one month timeline will be adequate to bring it on par with the older Air Force One planes.

Trump Said to Have Secretly Used Military Jet to Leave Turkey Amid Threats (New York Times)
Trump Switches Back To Qatari Plane After Leaving Turkey On Old Air Force One (Forbes)

sources.news_title: Trump secretly flew out of Turkiye after NATO summit because of Iran threat: report
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump secretly flew out of last month's NATO summit in Ankara, Turkiye, on an alternate military aircraft while the White House made it appear that the Republican president was flying on Air Force One, according to a report published by The Washington Post on Monday (August 10, 2026).
The Post said an Iranian assassination threat against Mr. Trump prompted the operation. The ruse was carried out as journalists and some White House staff members were led to believe they were on the same plane as the President as he began his journey back to Washington from the annual gathering of NATO country leaders.
The Post cited material reviewed by the newspaper, a U.S. official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the President’s travel. The Associated Press has not independently confirmed the report.
Flying in on Qatari-gifted jet
Mr. Trump had flown to the summit in a new Qatari-gifted and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet. But ahead of departing Turkiye, he said he would fly partway home on an older-model baby blue Air Force One plane instead.
The President at the time said the new luxury jet was being flown out ahead of his departure from Ankara to give some U.S. troops based in eastern England a chance to check out the new Air Force One.
Also read: West Asia war LIVE updates
In Ankara, Mr. Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras ahead of the plane flying to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in the United Kingdom.
However, according to the Post report, after boarding the legacy Air Force One jet, he was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane — an Air Force C-32A — via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies. Mr. Trump flew to Mildenhall on that smaller jet.
White House mum about ruse
The White House did not respond directly to questions about the Post report of the secret operation to whisk Mr. Trump out of the country on a third aircraft, or the reported elaborate ruse to make it appear he was on the baby blue Air Force One jet flying to Mildenhall.
“As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
The U.S. Secret Service declined to comment. The Air Force, which maintains the fleet of executive travel aircraft, referred questions to the White House.
Threats to Trump
While Mr. Trump was in Turkiye, the U.S. military conducted a series of large strikes in Iran in retaliation for its attacks on merchant shipping in the region.
The New York Times and CBS News reported last month that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a potential attack on the U.S. President or his jet, triggering additional precautions and the decision not to use the newly inaugurated aircraft gifted to Mr. Trump by Qatar for the first leg of Mr. Trump’s trip home from Ankara.
The swap had spurred questions about the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft, and Mr. Trump said last month after the trip that it would undergo additional upgrades.
Mr. Cheung on Monday maintained that the new, Qatari-gifted plane was “a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff.”
‘Unusual occurrence’
The new Post report on clandestinely putting Mr. Trump on a third aircraft and quietly whisking him out of the country adds a fresh layer to just how seriously concerned U.S. security officials were about the threat against Mr. Trump during the ongoing war with Iran.
Paul Eckloff, a former special agent with the Secret Service, said such an unusual move could either reflect actionable intelligence or an abundance of caution given volatility in the region with the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
“I would not say unprecedented, but it is an unusual occurrence,” Mr. Eckloff told The Associated Press.
The Post reported that to exit that plane without being seen by those uninvolved in the operation, Mr. Trump and several aides stepped aboard an airport catering truck, which was elevated planeside using hydraulics and positioned at a door on the opposite side of Air Force One’s entrance.
The small group of reporters who thought they were travelling with Mr. Trump were advised to lower their window shades ahead of takeoff.
After arriving at Mildenhall, news photographers captured images of Mr. Trump getting off the presidential plane — suggesting he reboarded Air Force One out of sight of the pack of journalists who thought they were travelling with him.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal called for a congressional investigation.
“It is unprecedented and it is surreal,” he said Monday on CNN, calling the incident “downright scary.”
After the brief visit to the base at Mildenhall, Mr. Trump boarded the new Air Force One aircraft to fly the rest of the way to Washington.
During a gaggle with reporters aboard the aircraft, Mr. Trump was asked directly if there was any credible threats on Air Force One by Iran.
“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” Mr. Trump said. He added to the traveling reporters, “But if I go, you go.”

The elaborate ruse, which involved hiding the US president in a catering truck, took place when Mr Trump was in Ankara for a NATO summit in July.
The operation was triggered by an Iranian assassination threat to Mr Trump, the Post reports.
US President Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Türkiye last month when the White House said he was flying aboard Air Force One, in an extraordinary move that involved hiding him in an airport catering truck, the Washington Post reports.
Mr Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but he unexpectedly used an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.
The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Türkiye.
Before departing Ankara, Mr Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, while the new plane stopped at the same base so US service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.
After Mr Trump boarded the old Air Force One in front of cameras in Ankara, he was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Post reported, citing a US official familiar with the operation and corroborating material it reviewed.
The deception operation was triggered by a credible Iranian assassination threat to Mr Trump, the Post reported.
A US official with knowledge of the deception plan also confirmed the operation to the New York Times.
A similar operation had taken place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.

sources.news_title: Trump's secret flight out of Türkiye revealed after Iran threat
sources.text:
President Donald Trump was secretly flown out of Türkiye aboard a military jet after U.S. officials determined that an Iranian threat against him was credible during last month's NATO summit, according to two senior U.S. officials familiar with the operation.
Trump and the public had been led to believe he left Türkiye on July 8 aboard an older version of Air Force One.
Instead, Trump was moved from that aircraft through a catering container and taken to a separate military plane that secretly flew him to Britain, one of the officials said.
The elaborate deception was designed to conceal Trump's whereabouts and prevent potential attackers from knowing which aircraft he was actually aboard.
Reporters traveling with Trump were not told about the switch.
They remained aboard the older Air Force One and flew to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in England, unknowingly serving as decoys while Trump traveled separately aboard a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, according to the officials.
The Washington Post previously reported that the C-32A was the aircraft that carried Trump from Türkiye to Britain.
The operation was an unusual instance in which journalists assigned to cover a sitting president were deliberately misled about his location.
Trump had arrived in Türkiye aboard a luxury Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar. The aircraft is being considered for future use as Air Force One but has raised security concerns because it lacks some of the defensive capabilities found on the older presidential aircraft.
Trump publicly said he would leave Türkiye aboard the older Air Force One "for old time's sake."
At the airport, cameras captured Trump boarding the older aircraft through its usual left-side door. Journalists accompanying him boarded through the rear.
But Trump did not actually leave the country on that plane.
According to a U.S. official, a catering container was positioned on the opposite side of the aircraft, away from reporters. Trump was moved through the container and taken to the waiting military aircraft.
The reporters remained aboard the older Air Force One, unaware that the president was traveling separately.
The plane landed at Mildenhall at 10:16 p.m., according to a pool report. About 40 minutes later, Trump appeared, having already been secretly transferred back to the older Air Force One.
He then walked across the tarmac to the Qatari aircraft, where reporters were waiting. Trump and the press pool boarded the newer plane and flew to Washington.
The operation was assembled within hours after U.S. officials determined that a threat from Iran was credible, according to an official familiar with the planning.
Trump was briefed while in Türkiye, and a small group of senior officials was involved, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The threat was not specifically tied to the Qatari aircraft. Officials said Trump was considered a target regardless of which plane he used.
The White House repeated a statement issued during the summit by communications director Steven Cheung, who said the administration used "distraction and misdirection" to counter threats against Trump.
The White House later reissued the statement without that phrase.
Former Secret Service agent Donald Mihalek said the agency has previously used decoy motorcades and flights to protect presidents, particularly in areas where there is a risk of combat.

"I'm number one on their list, before you," Trump told reporters. "But if I go, you go. Right?"
Trump has faced Iranian threats since ordering the 2020 killing of Gen. Qassim Suleimani during his first term. U.S. intelligence also warned during his 2024 campaign of potential Iranian plots against him, prompting increased security and occasional use of decoy aircraft.
The threats included an alleged murder-for-hire plot involving an Iranian proxy and the hacking of Trump campaign officials' accounts.
The secret flight came after reports raised questions about the security of the Qatari aircraft, angering Trump and prompting the Justice Department to subpoena journalists involved in reporting on the issue. Those subpoenas were later withdrawn after a federal judge criticized the process.

The swap had spurred questions about the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft, and Trump said last month after the trip that it would undergo additional upgrades.
Cheung on Monday maintained that the new, Qatari-gifted plane was “a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff.”
The new Post report on clandestinely putting Trump on a third aircraft and quietly whisking him out of the country adds a fresh layer to just how seriously concerned U.S. security officials were about the threat against Trump during the ongoing war with Iran.
Paul Eckloff, a former special agent with the Secret Service, said such an unusual move could either reflect actionable intelligence or an abundance of caution given volatility in the region with the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
“I would not say unprecedented, but it is an unusual occurrence,” said Eckloff.
The Post reported that to exit that plane without being seen by those uninvolved in the operation, Trump and several aides stepped aboard an airport catering truck, which was elevated planeside using hydraulics and positioned at a door on the opposite side of Air Force One’s entrance.
The small group of reporters who thought they were traveling with Trump were advised to lower their window shades ahead of takeoff.
After arriving at Mildenhall, news photographers captured images of Trump getting off the presidential plane — suggesting he reboarded Air Force One out of sight of the pack of journalists who thought they were traveling with him.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal called for a congressional investigation.
“It is unprecedented and it is surreal,” he said Monday on CNN, calling the incident “downright scary.”
After the brief visit to the base at Mildenhall, Trump boarded the new Air Force One aircraft to fly the rest of the way to Washington.
During a gaggle with reporters aboard the aircraft, Trump was asked directly if there was any credible threats on Air Force One by Iran.
“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” Trump said. He added to the traveling reporters, “But if I go, you go.”
___
AP writers Josh Boak, Aamer Madhani and Konstantin Toropin contributed reporting.

Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026
What you need to know

- US-Iran talks on peace and reopening Strait of Hormuz hit impasse

Keep reading for the latest developments in the war in Iran and wider conflict in the Middle East from Tuesday, August 11:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
US says forces fired on tanker in Gulf of Oman
US Central Command on Tuesday said its forces fired on a Panama-flagged tanker in the Gulf of Oman Tuesday after the vessel's crew ignored warnings to stop.
CENTCOM said the crew of a Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the M/V Vela Nova, disabling its steering.
The ship was said to be in violation of a US blockade of Iranian ports when attacked by the US chopper.
A CENTCOM post on X said the Vela Nova is "no longer transiting to Iran."
The statement went on to say that the US had redirected 55 commercial ships in violation of the blockade, adding that it had disabled three non-compliant vessels and boarded two more.
The US Navy currently has more than 15 warships deployed to the Arabian Sea, including two aircraft carriers and an amphibious assault ship.
Lebanon becomes first Middle East country to abolish death penalty
Lebanon's parliament voted to abolish capital punishment on Tuesday, making it the first country in the Middle East to do away with the death penalty.
The country has not carried out an execution since 2004, but until Monday had continued to hand out death sentences. In January, the rights group Amnesty International (AI) said that at least 85 individuals were in death row cells in Lebanon.
To date, death sentences have handed down for crimes such as murder, terrorism or espionage, which will now be punished with life sentences involving hard labor.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who attended Tuesday's parliamentary session, called the vote a "historic step" for Lebanon.
The European Union said Lebanon was "setting a powerful example for other countries in the Middle East and beyond," whereas UN rights chief Volker Türk called on Lebanon's neighbors "to follow its lead in ending this inhumane practice."
UN Special Coordinator for Lebanon Jean Arnault said the change "advances the country's adherence to international human rights standards and justice with human dignity."
Capital punishment is commonly meted out across the region, with Amnesty International documenting more than 2,000 executions in Iran last year and more than 350 in Saudi Arabia.
Israel, Venezuela renew consular ties after 17 years
Israel and Venezuela on Tuesday announced the resumption of consular ties after a diplomatic break of 17 years.
"Following talks held in recent weeks and days between Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia, Israel and Venezuela have agreed to renew consular relations," read a statement from Israel's Foreign Ministry.
"The talks resulted in an agreement to establish a coordination mechanism that will enable the provision of consular services to citizens of both countries."
Venezuela, along with Bolivia, broke off diplomatic relations with Israel in 2009 over an Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip.
Tuesday's announcement comes in the wake of generous Israeli disaster relief for Venezuelan earthquake victims.
It also comes as new Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodriguez's administration adopts a markedly more cooperative stance towards US President Donald Trump after he ordered the abduction and arrest of her predecessor, Nicolas Maduro.
A joint statement said both Israel and Venezuela recognize "the importance of the relationship between the State of Israel and the Jewish community residing in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, which serves as an important bridge of historic friendship between the two countries."
Syria sentences Assad to death in absentia
A Syrian court has sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia.
Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family. He and his family to Russia, where he was granted asylum. Moscow is understood to have refused to extradite the toppled dictator.
For more on the story, you can check out our article here.
Container ship reportedly hit by missile in Gulf of Oman
A container ship is believed to have been struck by a missile in the Gulf of Oman, according to maritime security sources.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received a report of an incident involving a commercial vessel and military forces, later correcting the vessel type from a tanker to a container ship.
Initial assessments identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged Vela Nova.
British maritime risk management group Vanguard and a separate maritime security source said the ship was believed to have been hit while sailing around 71 nautical miles (132 kilometers) off Pakistan's coast.
Three killed in reported Houthi attack on cargo ship
Three crew members have been killed in a reported Houthi attack on a commercial vessel near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Yemeni government-linked sources.
Two Yemeni coast guard sources and two military officials said the Iran-aligned group attacked a deck cargo ship on Tuesday.
Yemeni pro-government broadcaster Al Yumhuriya said the vessel was hit by a missile and that the dead were two Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian.
The ship's name and nationality were not immediately given.
Yemeni government sources said authorities were working to confirm the circumstances of the attack.
US has 'swept entire Strait of Hormuz' of mines: Trump
President Donald Trump said that the US has cleared the Strait of Hormuz of mines, and that the critical trade route was open to commercial traffic.
Trump told reporters at the White House that the US had 100% control of the waterway.
"A little bit complex because they [Iran] will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mines. You know, we've mine swept the entire Strait," he said.
Trump's comments came as Washington and Tehran have been negotiating the full reopening of the strait for some time. Iran has linked the route's reopening to concessions from the US and its allies while affirming plans to charge commercial vessels passing through the strait.
Trump responded to the concessions demand saying he too would demand compensation from Iran, for all the people injured or killed in the conflict.
Over the last weekend, US Vice President JD Vance said that Iran had laid a large number of mines in the Strait at he beginning of the war.
READ: Is Iran's middle class being pushed into poverty?
The war has intensified Iran's economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses.
Read DW's report on growing fears that millions of middle-income families in Iran are slipping closer to poverty.
Oil prices steady after increase, as hopes for a deal fade
Global crude oil prices steadied on Tuesday, after a significant rise amid persisting uncertainty over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude and US crude futures were both up slightly on Tuesday morning, reaching the highest levels since July 31, after the contracts spiked roughly 5% on Monday.
The price of Brent hovered just under $88 (€76) a barrel, having swing between $72 and $102 last month.
Oil prices have risen around 10% over the past week, fanning inflationary fears and revitalizing expectations of a possible US interest rate hike in 2026.
"We're now in a bit of a Mexican standoff, if you'd like, in terms of who blinks first," Tony Sycamore, a market Analyst at IG told Reuters.
"This is going to be almost a war of attrition now," he said. "You probably can see the (oil) market sitting around the $75 to $95 range while we wait to see who blinks first."
Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report
US President Donald Trump reportedly departed from Turkey on a secret military flight in July, instead of flying aboard an older Air Force One plane as announced by the White House.
This was in response to a credible Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported, as the monthslong war continued.
Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit in July. However, he unexpectedly announced he would used an older Air Force One when departing the country, "for old times's sake." The move had then raised questions over the donated jet's safety.
Trump boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras but was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Washington Post said, citing corroborating material and a US official familiar with the operation.
Journalists aboard the decoy Air Force One, where they believed they were to be accompanied by the US President, said they had been advised to keep their window shades closed in the press cabin.
When they inquired about it later, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight."
"But if I go, you go. Right?" he added.
The White House did not directly address the report.
Communications director Steven Cheung told the Post there were "many enemies of America" targeting Trump and that every available tool was being used to counter threats.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the war in Iran and developments from across the Middle East.
US President Donald Trump reportedly took a secret flight out of Turkey after the NATO summit in July, according to the Washington Post. The report describes how the US President was smuggled into a smaller plane, provoking mental visuals straight out of a Hollywood movie, to thwart a possible assassination attempt by Iran.
Trump meanwhile, has scoffed at Iran's demands of concessions and reparations, saying he too would seek conflict compensations as part of a peace deal. With this, negotiations over a truce and the possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz seem to have hit a wall once more.
The news had an effect on global markets as well, initially sending oil prices soaring, but they have now stabilized.

sources.news_title: Trump secretly switched to different plane in Turkey amid Iran missile threat
sources.text:
Trump secretly switched to different plane in Turkey amid Iran missile threat
Shortly before Air Force One took off from Turkey at the end of last month's NATO summit, President Trump secretly slipped away from the presidential jet and was whisked to another plane with the help of an airport catering truck, according to a U.S. official with direct knowledge of the matter.
The ruse was employed because the U.S. had learned of a threat from Iran and its allied proxies. U.S. intelligence had detected a credible plot to fire a missile at the plane Mr. Trump was on as he left the Turkish capital of Ankara, CBS News reported exclusively.
The president had expressed awareness of the risks posed by the U.S.-Iran war, calling himself Iran's "number one target" during the NATO summit.
The Washington Post was first to report on the secret plane-switching.
Multiple Trump administration officials expressed frustration Monday night that highly classified tactics and procedures leaked into the public eye, potentially limiting future protective operations for U.S. presidents.
Hours before the move, on July 8, Mr. Trump announced he would leave Ankara in the old Air Force One rather than a newer Qatari-donated jet that he had taken to the NATO summit. The president said he was switching planes "for old time's sake," and U.S. forces stationed at a U.K. refueling stop would be able to check out the new plane, but CBS News has reported that the Secret Service advised that he take the older plane for security reasons.
Video footage captured by the press showed the president walking up the stairs of the old Air Force One and disappearing into the plane, with a catering truck visible on the other side of the jet. Several minutes later, the truck pulled away and drove off to another U.S. government plane, which the Post reported was an Air Force C-32A.
Mr. Trump then flew from Ankara to a refueling stop in the United Kingdom on the separate plane while members of the press and the president's staff traveled the same route on Air Force One — and believed they were on board the same aircraft as the president.
While in Ankara, members of the press were told to keep the window shades in Air Force One's press cabin closed, reporters said at the time. Asked why the shades needed to be closed, Mr. Trump later told reporters they were "probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags that we have to deal with."
In the United Kingdom, Mr. Trump switched to the newer Air Force One, which was donated by the government of Qatar last year and retrofitted by the U.S. Air Force to serve as the new presidential plane. Mr. Trump spoke to members of the press while they flew across the Atlantic toward Washington, D.C.
The Trump administration has never publicly disclosed that the press and some members of the president's staff were flying on a decoy plane.
Last month, the new Air Force One — which debuted in June — was sent off to be "maxed out" with additional upgrades, the president told reporters, after questions arose about the newer plane's security features.
Asked Monday about the decision to secretly switch planes in Turkey, White House communications director Steven Cheung didn't respond directly to the question, saying in a statement: "The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff. As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats."
The Air Force has also called the new presidential plane "safe, secure and equipped with the most advanced technologies necessary to meet the requirements of the presidential mission."

sources.news_title: Trump Secretly Switched Planes In Turkey After Iran Threat, Report Says
sources.text:
Trump Secretly Switched Planes In Turkey After Iran Threat, Report Says
US President Donald Trump was secretly moved from the newly renovated Boeing 747 donated by Qatar to an older Air Force One aircraft during his recent visit to Turkey for the NATO summit after an Iranian threat prompted a last-minute change to his travel plans, The Washington Post reported.
Trump had arrived in Ankara aboard the Qatar-donated Boeing 747-8. He was expected to leave Turkey either on the same aircraft or on the older Air Force One.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
But on July 8, as tensions with Iran were rising, Trump was quietly transferred to a US Air Force C-32A, which later flew him to Britain, according to the report.
The switch was carried out away from public view at Ankara airport. Trump first boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras, while journalists and members of his delegation prepared to leave on the aircraft.
He was then reportedly moved into an airport catering truck, which drove across the airfield to the waiting C-32A, according to a US official and another person familiar with the president's travel arrangements cited by The Washington Post.
The smaller aircraft took off for Britain and landed at around 10.20 pm. The older Air Force One, carrying journalists and other personnel, arrived just minutes later, making it appear as though Trump had remained aboard the larger aircraft.
The move was notable because Trump had earlier said he planned to fly from Ankara to RAF Mildenhall in Britain aboard the older "baby blue" Air Force One, calling it a trip "for old time's sake".
He had also said the Qatar-donated aircraft would stop at the same British base, where US service members stationed there would get a chance to tour the newly refurbished plane.
Iranian Threat Prompted Aircraft Switch
The covert transfer sheds more light on why Trump did not leave Turkey aboard the Qatar-donated Boeing 747-8.
US media had previously reported that an Iranian threat was behind the decision, with some reports suggesting the possibility of threats from Iranian proxy groups. Turkey's border with Iran also added to the security concerns surrounding Trump's movements.
The security precautions continued after Trump boarded the older Air Force One. Journalists on the aircraft were reportedly instructed to keep their window blinds closed, a measure more commonly associated with flights through areas where security risks are elevated.
Video footage reviewed by The Washington Post also appeared to show a catering truck being lowered from the older Air Force One shortly after Trump boarded. The truck was later seen crossing the airfield towards the smaller C-32A parked farther away.
The incident has also raised fresh questions about the security capabilities of the Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar.
The aircraft carried Trump for the first time on July 1, when he travelled to North Dakota. It was later used for his trip to Turkey for the NATO summit.
Qatar's royal family donated the aircraft to the United States last year after Trump repeatedly criticised the ageing Boeing 747s that have served as Air Force One since 1990. The aircraft was subsequently given a rapid retrofit for presidential use.
However, The New York Times had previously reported that the plane initially lacked some of the defensive systems available on the older Air Force One, including anti-missile capabilities.
Trump was later filmed in Britain getting off the larger Air Force One before heading towards the newly retrofitted aircraft. It remains unclear how he was transferred back to the larger plane after arriving in Britain.
White House Defends New Aircraft
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung defended the security arrangements surrounding the Qatar-donated aircraft.
"The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff," Cheung said.
He added that Trump faces threats from multiple adversaries and that the administration uses "every tool at our disposal" to protect him.
The White House had issued a similar defence when questions were first raised about the security of the Qatar-donated aircraft.

Trump claims US controls Iranian money
President says Washington effectively acting as Tehran’s banker as 2 countries remain locked in conflict
President Donald Trump claimed on Tuesday that the United States had “total control” over Iran’s money, with Washington effectively acting as Tehran’s banker as the two countries remain locked in a military conflict.
“We control their money, what they had, which is a lot,” Trump said in an interview with TV host Wayne Allyn Root. “We have total control of it. I’m their banker. I am their banker.”
Trump described Iran’s economy as being in severe distress. “They’ve got 300% inflation. They have no value. Their currency has almost no value. They have they they're not paying their soldiers. Their soldiers are leaving. So just keep that going. It's not sustainable,” he said.
The president outlined three possible approaches toward Iran: maintaining current pressure, striking the country “really, really hard” or relying primarily on economic pressure.
“We could just keep it alone, and they're going to fail. We could just keep, you know, doing sort of just like nice and easy, relaxed. Like I said, some sort of negotiator. You see, they are very devious negotiators because they'll agree to something, then they'll go out and tell the press that they did not do it. They're very dishonest people. So we have three strategies,” said Trump.
.@POTUS on Iran: "They're very devious negotiators because they'll agree to something, then they'll go out and tell the press that they never agreed to it. They're very dishonest people." pic.twitter.com/zxf9B4lbM9
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) August 11, 2026
“So just keep that going. It's not sustainable. Hit them really, really hard. Or this, this. I think really the third is just bear economically. But we're doing that anyway. That's sort of a part of the question,” he added.
When asked how the conflict could end, Trump said his primary objective was preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“I’m in this thing for one primary reason: that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” he said, claiming US military action had prevented Tehran from acquiring one.
Qatar says Iran-Oman Hormuz talks reached ‘advanced stage,’ urges reopening
Qatar said on Tuesday that negotiations between Iran and Oman on arrangements for the Strait of Hormuz have reached “an advanced stage,” expressing hope the strategic waterway will reopen “as soon as possible.”
Speaking at a press conference, Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said the talks were at a “critical juncture” and stressed that Doha supports all efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region.
“As mediators, we want the Strait of Hormuz reopened as soon as possible,” Ansari said.
He said Qatar was closely following the negotiations and remained supportive of diplomatic efforts to reach an agreement.
Iran and Oman have been negotiating legal and technical arrangements for navigation through the strait after maritime traffic was disrupted following the military conflict between Iran and the US. Tehran has said implementation of any reopening is linked to resolving disputes over what it describes as US violations of the June memorandum of understanding.
US ‘begged' Iran for negotiations, says FM Araghchi
The Iranian foreign minister, speaking at a televised news conference on Iranian state television, said that the US “begged” Iran to negotiate, Al Jazeera reported on Tuesday.
He recalled that US President Donald Trump demanded “unconditional surrender” from Iran at the beginning of the war.
“The US President wrote two words [on social media] at the beginning of the war: ‘Unconditional surrender’,” he said.
“That was what they wanted from us and, 20 days later, the same enemy was begging for negotiations,” the top diplomat added.
In the same press conference, Araghchi also said that Iran showed the world that it is “a tough and invincible power,” Al Jazeera reported.
Speaking at a televised press conference, he said: “I have heard this many times from foreign ministers and officials from other countries: ‘You Iranians created a miracle; you surprised the whole world.’”
“No one thought that Iran could resist America like this,” Araghchi said, adding that the US had the backing of Israel, the Western world and some other countries.
Abbas Araghchi and his German counterpart Johann Wadephul held a phone conversation earlier on Monday, where Araghchi said that insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz was solely the result of military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran, according to IRNA.
Araghchi briefed Wadephul on ongoing consultations with Oman aimed at establishing a safe route for maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian foreign minister said, and Wadephul also discussed bilateral relations as well as regional and international developments.
He called on the international community to hold the US administration accountable for the security and economic consequences of the Strait of Hormuz’s closure.
Araghchi emphasised that restoring security in the waterway requires an end to US aggressive actions and unlawful interference, including a maritime blockade and other violations of US commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Iran condemns Israeli attacks on Lebanon, blames UNSC silence
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei condemned recent Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon, saying the silence of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) has encouraged further Israeli aggression, according to IRNA.
Baghaei said on Tuesday that continued Israeli attacks had resulted in the martyrdom and injuries of Lebanese civilians and caused damage to homes and infrastructure.
The spokesperson criticised the international community’s silence and inaction, particularly by the UNSC, saying they had emboldened the Israeli regime to continue violating Lebanon’s territorial integrity and national sovereignty.
He also condemned the US administration for being an accomplice in Israeli crimes across Lebanon, the occupied Palestinian territories and the wider region because of its comprehensive support for the Israeli regime.
Baghaei praised the Lebanese people for their resistance and resilience against Israeli aggression and occupation, stressing Iran’s full solidarity with Lebanon in defending its sovereignty, dignity and independence.
Israeli warplanes reportedly struck areas around Al-Mansouri Municipality in southern Lebanon’s Tyre District, while Israeli artillery targeted the Ali al-Taher Hill in Nabatiyeh Governorate.
Israeli drone shells ambulance teams in southern Lebanon despite US deal
An Israeli drone targeted ambulance teams on Tuesday while they were evacuating an injured person in Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, in the latest violation of a US-mediated framework agreement, Lebanese media said.
The drone shelled ambulance crews from the Islamic Health Authority, Bayt al-Talaba and the Islamic Risala Scout Association as they were transferring a person injured in an earlier strike on a car in the area, the state-run National News Agency reported.
Several ambulances were damaged in the attack, but there were no immediate reports of injuries among paramedics.
Earlier Tuesday, the agency reported that an Israeli drone dropped explosive and incendiary materials on the outskirts of Kfar Rumman, adjacent to Nabatieh, without giving details about casualties or damage.
The attack came despite the US-mediated framework agreement signed by Beirut and Tel Aviv in late June. The framework agreement calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups, referring to Hezbollah.
3 crew members killed after Houthi attack on commercial vessel in Bab al-Mandeb
Three crew members were killed after Yemen’s Houthi group attacked a commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a government-affiliated broadcaster reported on Tuesday.
Al-Jumhuriya TV said two Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian were killed according to preliminary information.
The broadcaster did not identify the vessel or its owner.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Bab al-Mandeb is the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran to restore 95 mcm/day of gas production by end-September
Iran will restore 95 million cubic metres (mcm) per day of gas production capacity by the end of September, the oil ministry said on Tuesday, as Tehran repairs energy infrastructure damaged during the war with Israel and the United States.
In July, a senior government official said Iran expected to restore about 100 mcm per day of natural gas production capacity "within the coming months", after strikes cut output by about 230 mcm/day since the war started in late February.
Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad was quoted by the ministry's news outlet as saying 95 mcm/day of lost capacity would return following damage to gas-processing facilities in Assaluyeh.
He said the impact had largely been offset by using spare capacity at other gas-processing plants.
Reconstruction of four damaged gas-processing plants was advancing rapidly, Paknejad said, adding debris had been cleared, reconstruction systems were in place and contractors had begun work.
He said rebuilding was expected to finish ahead of schedule, allowing the full lost capacity to return to the production network.
Some of the restored capacity would nevertheless be unavailable during the winter, Paknejad said, meaning Iran would need to manage both gas supply and consumption carefully to avoid challenges in meeting demand.
Trump left Turkiye on secret flight amid Iranian threat: report
US President Donald Trump secretly departed Türkiye on a military aircraft last month amid an alleged Iranian assassination threat against him while the White House publicly said he was aboard Air Force One, US media reported on Monday, citing a US official and other sources familiar with the operation.
According to The Washington Post, Trump boarded the older Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras in Ankara before being quietly transferred minutes later to a smaller Air Force C-32A using an airport catering truck.
The report described the manoeuvre as designed to conceal his location from the public, journalists and some White House staff members.
The operation came a night after US forces renewed strikes on Iran following a breakdown in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
Trump visited Ankara for a NATO summit on July 7-8 with world leaders when the alleged threat emerged.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung defended the measures, saying the Qatari-gifted aircraft, which is now used as Air Force One, has been "fitted with high-level security protocols" to ensure the president's safety.
“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” he added.
Oil prices jump 5% as Trump keeps Iran escalation option open
Oil prices jumped around 5% on Monday after US President Donald Trump said a “massive escalation” against Iran remained an option, deepening uncertainty over negotiations to end the conflict and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
International benchmark Brent crude rose 5% to $87.7 per barrel as of 2005GMT, its highest level in nearly two weeks, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) climbed 5.1% to $82.2.
Read: Trump demands compensation from Iran for alleged atrocities of past 50 years
Brent extended its gains for a fourth consecutive trading session as markets assessed the prospects of further military action and continued disruption to energy shipments through the strategic waterway.
Asked whether a major escalation against Iran remained under consideration, Trump said Washington could pursue that option.
“Well, we have that certain ability if we want to do that,” he told reporters at the White House.
Trump also said Iran should pay compensation for damage caused over the past 50 years, rejecting Tehran’s demands for war compensation in negotiations.
While Trump claimed that the Strait of Hormuz was open and “100%” controlled by the US, he acknowledged that Iran could still attempt to disrupt maritime traffic.
Tehran has said Washington must lift its blockade before Iran agrees to fully reopen the waterway, through which a significant share of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passes.
Prices were also supported by reports of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery and a tanker operated by Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. over the weekend.
Meanwhile, crude stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell below 300 million barrels to about 298.7 million last week, their lowest level since 1983.
US continues withdrawing tanker aircraft from Israel’s Ben Gurion airport: Israeli media
The number of US aerial refuelling aircraft stationed at Ben Gurion Airport in central Israel has declined, nearing levels seen during a previous ceasefire, Israeli Channel 12 reported on Monday.
“The Americans continue to reduce the number of refuelling aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport” near Tel Aviv, the broadcaster said.
The number of tanker aircraft had “already approached” levels seen during the ceasefire, when about 20 such aircraft were stationed at the airport, it added.
The channel did not provide the number of aircraft at the height of tensions.
The report comes as reports have circulated in recent days that the US and Iran could be nearing an agreement on outstanding issues, particularly navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies and trade.
US aircraft have been stopping at Ben Gurion for aerial refuelling since the US-Israeli war on Iran began February 28.
Channel 12 reported Sunday that the US Air Force “had begun withdrawing some of its refuelling aircraft stationed at Ben Gurion Airport amid security developments.”
The move came after Israeli Transport Minister Miri Regev pressed security officials to remove the tanker aircraft to maintain normal airport operations during peak travel days, the channel added.
According to the channel, more than 2.6 million passengers are expected to pass through the airport in August, averaging about 100,000 passengers a day, making it the busiest month since October 7, 2023, as August is a popular vacation period for Israelis.
There was no immediate comment from Washington or Tel Aviv on the report.
Israel has previously debated the impact of US tanker aircraft stationed at Ben Gurion on civilian flight operations.
On July 14, Israel barred additional US aerial refuelling aircraft from landing at Ben Gurion after their number reached 33. Regev said the aircraft were occupying spaces needed for civilian planes.
The US Central Command, or CENTCOM, objected to the decision the same day. Israel reversed the decision on July 15 following US protests.
Trump demands compensation from Iran for alleged atrocities of past 50 years
President Donald Trump on Monday declined to say what would come next in talks with Iran, but indicated that the US retains the ability to pursue a major military escalation.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “You’ll find out, when asked what would follow the latest round of negotiations, which he had previously described as Iran’s “last chance” before possible military action.
Read more: Trump says US taking 'low-key' approach to Iran, stresses Tehran's economic pain
Asked whether a “massive escalation” remained on the table, Trump said the US can pursue such an option if he chooses to do so.
“Well, we have that certain ability if we want to do that,” Trump said. “Yeah, you’ll find out.”
The president said the US is going to ask for money for the damage Iran has done over 50 years.
"If there's damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages," he added.
'We've mine swept the entire strait'
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said the strategic waterway is “open.”
"Well, it's open now ... The only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy. We have a blockade that's been infallible. It's a steel wall, and we let people in that we want to let in, and those people come in, and they've been coming in and they're going out, so it's actually open now. We do not let them go into Iran. They're not admitted into the strait to go to Iran, but it's open for others now," Trump said.
He acknowledged that Iran could still attempt to disrupt shipping, saying Iranian forces could “on occasion, drop a mine,” but claimed US forces have located and cleared mines throughout the strait.
"You know, we've mine swept the entire strait, as you probably maybe heard, maybe you didn't hear. But we control the strait 100%. Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble, but they're broke. They have no money," Trump said.
Hopes for Hormuz deal fade as Trump demands Iranian reparations
US President Donald Trump on Monday responded to Iran's conditions for a peace deal with his own demands that Iran pay compensation for people killed in wars, attacks and protests, in a rhetorical escalation likely to complicate efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump's proposal, which had not been raised before, was a response to Tehran's demands for compensation and an end to sanctions. The Iranian demands were largely in line with the terms of a preliminary peace deal signed in June, which has since broken down.
Also read: Iran says framework agreed with Oman on Strait of Hormuz
Since the war began in February, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.
"We're going to ask for money for the damage they've done over a 50-year period," Trump said at the White House, saying payments would cover deaths among both civilian demonstrators and US forces in the region.
"So if there's damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages," Trump said.
Trump cites attack blamed on Al Qaeda, not Iran
Referring to Tehran's crackdown on foreign-funded and incited protests in late 2025 and 2026, Trump claimed with no evidence that Iran had killed some 52,000 protesters as of six weeks ago. While some Iranian opposition and exile groups have echoed the claims of tens of thousands killed, the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) in February claimed around 7,000 deaths including 6,500 protesters.
Trump encouraged protesters to overthrow the Iranian government when the war began with US and Israeli airstrikes on civilian targets in February.
Trump also said Iran should compensate families of the 17 US sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on the naval vessel USS Cole, which has been blamed on al Qaeda, not Iran.
"Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Iran earlier said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz but repeated that the US must meet conditions, including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats before the key waterway is reopened.
The strait, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed prior to the conflict, has been effectively blocked since the war began, pushing up oil prices and inflation.
Trump under pressure
Ironically, the agreement with Oman would give Tehran more leverage over the key waterway than it had before the war began.
Trump is under pressure to end a war that is deeply unpopular at home ahead of midterm elections in November, and high fuel prices are a top issue in rural areas that have backed him in the past.
"What you're seeing here is the beginning of a capitulation," Democratic US Representative Bill Keating said on CNN. "This is reality. It's sinking in."
Earlier on Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said talks with Oman were "progressing smoothly and constructively", with an agreement reached on a shipping route map, while some technical issues remained unresolved.
Baghaei said the discussions also covered services which would normally involve payment, such as safe navigation, environmental protection, maritime services and combating crime.
US officials have repeatedly ruled out any deal that would allow Tehran to charge fees for access to the strait.
But months of US military efforts, including a two-week campaign of strikes in July, have not broken Iran's grip on the strait, despite Trump's misleading claim, repeated on Monday, that the strait was open and, "The only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy."
Washington and Tehran agreed to a ceasefire in June, but the US reimposed a blockade on Iranian shipping in July, a move that Tehran said violated the truce.
Iran has been striking back with missiles and drones against Washington's allies in the region, while also targeting commercial ships transiting the strait without its permission.

Trump flew secretly from Turkiye due to Iranian threat, the Washington Post reports
- The Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board
President Trump secretly departed Turkey on a military flight due to an Iranian assassination threat, while a decoy Air Force One carried press, an extraordinary security measure.
- Trump's secret flight from Turkey
- Iranian assassination threat
- Decoy Air Force One operation
- Presidential security measures
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Turkiye last month when the White House said he was flying aboard Air Force One, an extraordinary move prompted by an Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported Monday.
Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but he unexpectedly used an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane’s security.
The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkiye.
Before departing Ankara, Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older baby blue Air Force One plane “for old time’s sake” to RAF Mildenhall in Britain while the new plane stopped at the same base so US service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.
After Trump boarded the old Air Force One in front of cameras in Ankara, he was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Post reported citing a US official familiar with the operation and corroborating material it reviewed.
KSA, Turkiye, Pakistan sign defence deal
The deception operation was triggered by a credible threat to Trump, the Post reported.
A similar operation had taken place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.
On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were traveling with Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed.
The Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.
When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Trump said it was because they were “probably on a dangerous flight.”
He went onto say: “But if I go, you go. Right?“ The C-32A carrying Trump flew to Britain, arriving at around 10:20 p.m. with the older Air Force One and media, arriving minutes later, the Post reported. It was not clear, the paper said, how Trump was moved from the C-32A back to the older Air Force One.
Trump’s traveling press pool reported he climbed down the stairs of the older Air Force One at 10:56 p.m. local time.
He gave press a peace sign but didn’t walk over to talk to them.
He then spent some time greeting service members before walking to the new, Qatar-donated plane.
When asked for comment on the revelation of a secret flight on a third plane, the White House provided a statement from Communications Director Steve Cheung saying the Qatari-donated jet has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.
“As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,”
Cheung said. It was the same statement provided to the Post.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
